tasks.goal: open the middle drawer of the cabinet

rounds.weakness: The pull was one open-loop linear move at constant speed. On a stiff drawer (damping 3000 N*s/m) the handle slid out of the pinch grasp after a few millimetres, the hand finished its motion empty, the API reported the motion as 'ok', and the pipeline believed it had pulled; all 3 retries repeated the same slip (travel ~0 on 10/10 seeds).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the articulated part moves freely and follows the hand). Real drawers stick and vary in stiffness, and the pipeline never compared where the hand went with where the drawer went.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the drawer follows the hand perfectly, so a successful motion status was taken as evidence that the object moved; no grasp check after closing and no progress check during the pull.
rounds.fix: Check gripper_holding() after closing (re-approach if empty); pull in 1 cm increments relative to the current hand pose (bounded force), after each increment check the grasp and the measured drawer travel (averaged detections), stop on slip or stall, then re-detect the handle and re-grasp from where the drawer now is (up to 4 attempts).
rounds.general_rule: When moving an object through contact, command small increments relative to the current measured pose and verify after each that the object itself moved and is still held; never infer object motion from the robot's own motion status.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline only planned around the scene: with a tall movable box standing where the hand must end up after the pull, every pre-grasp and pull step was refused as a collision (or the hand stopped on the force limit), on 10/10 seeds. It had no notion of the volume its own task motion needs, nor of rearranging movable clutter. During repair two more weaknesses appeared: a single-detection top grasp on a narrow object landed a finger on its rim and the object slipped out unnoticed, and the first 'free' spot chosen was in the forearm's sweep.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A6 (nothing stands in the volume swept by the hand and arm while approaching and pulling). Real drawers have things parked in front of them, and the pipeline's tilted-approach trick only avoids clutter that is low.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene only low objects (plate) were near the drawer, and the planner's collision avoidance silently handled them, so the work volume was never made explicit.
rounds.fix: Before grasping the handle, compute the work volume (pull path plus palm/forearm margin) from the detected handle and pull direction; every non-cabinet obstacle that intrudes above handle height - 5 cm is picked (top grasp from 20-sample averaged detections) and placed on the nearest free table spot that is clear of other obstacles, of the work volume and of the base-to-hand forearm band; lifting is verified (object rose with the hand, still held) and the scene is re-checked after placing, with up to 3 tries.
rounds.general_rule: Before executing a contact motion, derive the full volume the robot will sweep (hand, palm and forearm, over the whole motion), and if a movable object intrudes, relocate it to a spot outside that volume and verify it moved, instead of hoping the planner finds a way around.

rounds.weakness: The work volume was checked for blockers exactly once, at the start. A box that slid into the space in front of the drawer one second later was never noticed: every pull step was refused as a collision and the retry loop just re-grasped the handle and tried the same blocked pull again (s_break 0.0). Repair exposed two more bugs: the work volume was recomputed from the current (partly opened) handle, so it drifted outward and swallowed every free table spot; and single noisy obstacle boxes flagged a low bowl as a blocker at random.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A8 (the scene is static after the first look). The pipeline cached the result of one perception pass and acted on it for the whole episode, and real workspaces change while the robot works (people put things down, objects slide).
rounds.why_missed: In all earlier scenes nothing moved on its own, so a single look was sufficient and the retry loop only ever retried the robot's own failure, not a changed scene.
rounds.fix: Every attempt now starts with fresh perception: re-detect the handle, re-check the work volume (computed from the closed-drawer reference = current handle minus measured travel), wait until blockers stop moving (averaged track windows), then clear them; a refused pull step ends the attempt so the next one re-perceives. Obstacle boxes are averaged over 8 calls before thresholding.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive before every attempt and every phase of a multi-step manipulation, derive safety volumes from fixed task references rather than from state that your own actions change, and treat a refused or blocked motion as a sign the scene changed, not as a reason to repeat the same motion.

rounds.weakness: The handle was only ever approached in the vertical plane of the pull axis (pitch varied, yaw never), so a fixed post standing just beyond the opened drawer front blocked the palm/forearm for every candidate approach. Worse, the clearing step tried to pick up the fixed post again and again (3 grasps per attempt, every attempt) and burned the whole 3000-step budget (10/10 seeds hit the step limit). Repair also showed the post-release retreat went along the pull direction, straight into the obstacle.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A4 (the space straight in front of and above the handle is free). The approach family had only one degree of freedom and the clutter-clearing step from round 2 silently assumed every obstacle is movable.
rounds.why_missed: Every earlier blocker was either low (avoided by pitching down) or movable (relocated), so the approach family and the 'clear it' strategy were never confronted with something that can be neither stepped over nor moved.
rounds.fix: Approach candidates now vary yaw (0, +-30, +-55 deg) as well as pitch; each candidate is scored by sampling fingers, palm (wide along the closing axis) and wrist at the current, half-open and fully-open grip poses against averaged obstacle boxes, and collision-free candidates are tried first. An obstacle that is held but does not rise when lifted is marked immovable and never re-grasped (it is planned around instead). After releasing the handle the hand retreats back along its own approach axis.
rounds.general_rule: When something is in the way, first test whether it can be moved (and remember the answer); for what cannot be moved, search over the full set of approach directions and check the whole hand-and-wrist sweep of the planned motion against it before committing, and always retreat along the direction you came in.

rounds.weakness: With the cabinet turned to face the robot (and moved), the drawer has to be pulled toward the robot base, so the hand's work volume now ran through the bowl, the wine bottle and next to the wine rack. The clearing step tried to top-grasp the 27 cm rack three times per attempt (force-limit hits), spent its tries on table spots the arm could not reach next to the rack, and the steep 35-45 deg approaches it fell back to drove the open upper finger into the drawer front; every seed ran out of steps (s_break 0.0). Repair also exposed that a bowl wider than the gripper can only be picked by its rim, and that a single failed grasp was being treated as 'immovable'.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A2/A3 (the cabinet stands where it usually does, facing sideways). A real robot meets furniture in other poses, and everything the pipeline derived (approach family, which clutter matters, where to put it) had only ever been exercised in one layout.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal and earlier layouts the pull went sideways across open table, the only clutter in the work volume was a narrow box, and the 25-deg approach always worked first, so the gripper-geometry limits (opening width, finger reach past the handle standoff) and the reachability of placement spots were never tested.
rounds.fix: Approach candidates are scored by sampled hand/wrist collisions (fingers, palm, wrist out to 35 cm) and all are tried in order (refusals cost no time); tilts capped at 25 deg because the open finger must not reach past the handle standoff. Clearing: objects much wider than the gripper are not attempted; objects slightly wider are pinched at the rim nearest the robot; a refused placement switches to a spot at least 15 cm away (up to 4 spots); held-but-not-lifting marks immovable only for normal grasps; after one full failed clearing an object is remembered as immovable and planned around. The work-volume height threshold now reflects the palm's reach below the handle (8 cm).
rounds.general_rule: Before acting on an object, check the action's preconditions against the gripper's own geometry (opening width, finger length and reach) and the arm's reach, choose a grasp mode that fits (body, edge, or none), and bound the tries per object with memory of what failed, so a strategy tuned in one layout degrades into planning around rather than burning the time budget in another.

tasks.goal: push the plate to the front of the stove

rounds.weakness: The only transport primitive was a two-finger pinch on the plate's thin, slanted rim lip followed by lifting that edge. With a realistic 0.4 kg plate the pinch slips immediately (36 'dropped' events in 10 seeds, success 0/10). The pipeline had no non-prehensile fallback: closed fingers pushing from inside ride over the shallow rim cone, pushing from outside requires putting the hand on the cabinet side where there is no room, and tilted-finger pushes swept the arm into a neighbouring bowl.
rounds.how_found: Questioned F1 (the plate is light enough to lift by its lip). In simulation it weighs 11 g, 30x lighter than a real plate, and the whole strategy rested on that number.
rounds.why_missed: I picked the strategy by probing the simulated object and kept whatever moved it; the probes all used the simulated mass, so 'lift by the lip' looked reliable and I never asked whether it scales to a realistic weight. Pushing had been tried first and abandoned for geometric reasons, so no push primitive survived to fall back on.
rounds.fix: None accepted. Tried six repairs: drag-in-hops (pinch, lift the edge 2-8 cm so the far edge stays on the table, drag 8-16 cm, release, re-detect), different pinch-angle orderings and speeds; best 0.5 on v1 with base dropping to 0.7. Hops are bimodal (either ~10 cm of progress or a slip with none) and the episode step budget runs out. Pipeline reverted to the round-0 version.
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a grasp-and-lift strategy for an object, check that it still works when the object's mass and friction are scaled to real-world values, and keep a non-prehensile or support-sharing fallback whose required force does not depend on grip friction.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline treated the goal region as a fixed place to put the plate and only chose the least-occupied point inside it. When a movable cup stood in the middle of the region, every candidate point overlapped it, so the plate was dropped onto or against the cup and ended tilted or pushed out (0/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3/D2 (some part of the goal is free). A small low block (rejected6) was simply shoved aside by the plate (0.6), so I used a taller, heavier movable object that cannot be shoved or covered.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the goal region was empty except for a nearby cheese box, so choosing the clearest point inside it always worked; I designed the target choice to avoid obstacles, not to remove them.
rounds.fix: Added clear_goal(): if the best target point still has negative clearance, find the movable object (a name in objects(), not a fixture part) blocking it, grasp it, and place it on a free table spot that is clear of other objects, of the whole goal region (not just the chosen point) and of the plate's carry corridor, and within comfortable reach. A first version kept the spot clear of only the chosen point and the cup landed where the plate later had to go (0.7 -> 0.9 after fixing).
rounds.general_rule: Before placing an object at a goal, check that the goal area is actually free; if it is occupied by something movable, relocate the blocker to a spot clear of the whole goal area and of the planned path first.

rounds.weakness: The goal-clearing step from round 2 assumed any blocker can be picked up with a top grasp. A 10 cm wide box (wider than the 8 cm gripper opening) could not be grasped, so the goal stayed blocked and the plate was dropped onto the box (0/10). Two hidden weaknesses showed up during repair: the 'plate is lifted' check (detected height above rest) was fooled when the plate came to rest on top of another object, and a pushed-away blocker that ended near the plate's swing path knocked the hanging plate out of the pinch.
rounds.how_found: Read the new clear_goal() code and questioned the assumption it introduced (the blocker fits between the fingers). Wide flat things such as boxes, books or cutting boards are common on real tables.
rounds.why_missed: The fix in round 2 was written for the one blocker I had just seen (a cup), so the removal primitive was chosen to suit that object and not checked against the gripper's size limit.
rounds.fix: clear_goal() now compares the blocker's smaller horizontal side with the gripper span; if it is too wide (or the grasp fails) it is pushed away with the closed fingers (wide finger face against it). The push direction is the one with the shortest travel that ends clear of other objects, of the whole goal region and of the plate's carry corridor, with a reachable start and end; if none qualifies the limits are relaxed. The carry loop now checks that the plate followed the hand (displacement ratio), not only that it is above the table, and the push is scored to end far from the corridor because the dangling plate swings up to a diameter away from the hand.
rounds.general_rule: When a skill has to handle an arbitrary object (remove, grasp, move), check the object's size against the gripper's capacity and keep a non-grasping alternative, and confirm that a carried object is really attached by checking that it moved with the hand.

rounds.weakness: The rim pinch only considered whether the planner could reach a rim segment; it never looked at what stood around the plate. With four cans 3 cm from the rim, most pinch approaches were refused, the remaining ones (on the cabinet side) carried the plate across the cans, and the dangling plate came to rest on top of them (s_break 0.4, from 0.6 with three cans).
rounds.how_found: Questioned E1/A2 (the space around the rim is free for the open fingers and for the swinging plate). Real tables are cluttered, and a pinch on a wide object needs room outside its edge.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the only neighbours were a bowl on one side and the cabinet on another, and trying 8 pinch angles was enough to find a free one. I treated failed approaches as something to retry at other angles, not as a sign that the surroundings had to be changed.
rounds.fix: Added declutter(): before the first transfer (and again whenever no rim pinch works) every small movable object within 5 cm of the plate rim or inside the plate's carry corridor is picked up and placed on a free spot (clear of other objects, the goal region, the plate and the corridor). The pick-and-place code was factored out of clear_goal(). A first version only decluttered reactively after all pinches failed; that kept the cans in the carry path (0.5). Doing it before the transfer gave 0.8-0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Before manipulating an object, clear small movable clutter from both the volume the gripper needs around the grasp point and the volume the object will sweep while carried; do not rely on trying other grasp angles.

rounds.weakness: The pinch point was a hard-coded radius (6.7 cm) and depth (5 mm) tuned on the nominal plate. On a plate scaled to 0.7 the pinch point lies outside the plate and every grasp closed on air (0/10). After deriving radius and depth from the measured bounding box, a second limit showed up: the scaled lip is only 1.3 cm tall, and the grip site cannot go much lower than 1.2-1.7 cm above the table before the finger tips hit it (the planner refuses). The pads therefore barely overlap the lip and the plate slips out when lifted.
rounds.how_found: Questioned B3 (fixed size). A scale of 1.3 (rejected1) did not break it, because a constant radius still lands on the wider rim; the smaller side was the real weakness.
rounds.why_missed: I tuned the constants by probing one plate. The bigger-plate test passed, so I wrongly concluded that the size assumption was harmless and never tested the smaller side.
rounds.fix: None accepted (pipeline reverted). The six repairs are listed in v5.yaml; the best reached 0.5. A low, thin lip needs a different primitive (a side or angled pinch, or a push) that the top-down pinch cannot provide.
rounds.general_rule: Derive grasp points and depths from the object's measured size rather than constants, and before relying on a grasp check that the part to be gripped is taller than the gripper's minimum clearance above the support surface; test size changes in both directions.

rounds.weakness: Every pinch needs a vertical top-down approach with the 20 cm long hand aligned with the rim's radius. A fixed board 7.5 cm above the table over the far half of the plate makes every such pose collide (0/10, 'no rim grasp' 40 times). The pipeline has no grasp that works from the side or at an angle, and no way to pull the plate out from under the board first.
rounds.how_found: Questioned E1 (the space above the rim is free). Shelves, cupboard bottoms and other robot links often cover part of an object on a real robot.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal scene had nothing above table height near the plate, so I only reasoned about the footprint of the hand (the fingers), not about the hand's full length at the height where it sits.
rounds.fix: None (unsolved). A sweep of the planner over all rim angles and hand yaws found no collision-free pinch pose. Recovering would need a new primitive (an angled or side pinch, or a hook-and-pull of the rim) that this pipeline does not have.
rounds.general_rule: When choosing a grasp, check that the whole hand (not just the finger tips) fits in the free space above the grasp point, and keep at least one grasp or contact primitive whose approach direction is not vertical.

rounds.weakness: The top grasp only varied the grasp point and wrist tilt around the object. With the object lying 7 mm from a 5 cm tall container wall, the hand body (about 20 cm wide along the finger-closing axis, only ~4 cm above the grip point) collided with the wall for every candidate, so the planner refused all descents and the program gave up without touching anything.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (free space beside the object along the closing axis). In Phase 1 two seeds already needed a lateral shift and a tilt to fit next to the bowl, which showed the margin was only a few millimetres.
rounds.why_missed: I thought of clearance as finger clearance (the opening is 8 cm vs a 4.3 cm object), not hand clearance, and assumed the scene always leaves room for some top-down approach; the official init states happen to keep about 6-9 cm between the two objects.
rounds.fix: When every grasp candidate is refused, relocate the blocker: pick the nearest small movable neighbour by its far-side wall, carry it to the free spot (scored with all obstacle boxes, validated by the planner) and set it down, then grasp again. Also: try both lateral shift directions, re-check holding after the lift, and use obstacle boxes (fixture parts included) instead of object centres for neighbour distances. Pushing or dragging the object itself was tried first and was unreliable (fingertip drag slips by friction balance; end pushes along the long axis did not move it far enough from a round wall and ran into a low stove).
rounds.general_rule: When no collision-free grasp exists because a movable neighbour is in the way of the hand (not just the fingers), move the neighbour away first (or change the scene) instead of only varying the grasp pose; and estimate clearance with the full hand geometry along the closing axis, not the finger opening.

rounds.weakness: The place target (the container) was detected once, right after the lift, and the hand then flew to that stale position and released. When the container slid ~10 cm during the carry, the object was dropped on the table where the container had been.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A8 (the place target does not move after detection). The detection happens 4-5 s before the release, which is a long open-loop window for anything a person or another robot might touch.
rounds.why_missed: I treated perception as a one-shot step before motion, and the noise-averaging I added made the single snapshot feel trustworthy; nothing in the base scene ever moves.
rounds.fix: place_in_container(): re-detect the container (averaged) after moving above it and again after the descent; if it moved more than 2 cm, re-target and repeat (lifting first if already low), up to 6 times, before opening the gripper.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive the goal location immediately before every irreversible step (release, insertion, contact) and re-target if it moved, instead of acting on a detection taken before a long motion.

rounds.weakness: Every grasp candidate used a vertical (straight-down) gripper. With the object at the far edge of the workspace (0.83 m from the base) there is no IK solution for a vertical wrist at table height, so every candidate was refused; the program then misdiagnosed this as 'blocked by a neighbour', relocated an unrelated object, and its relative lift-after-failure accumulated until targets left the workspace bounds. Once the object was held, a carry that stopped half-way dropped it and the program released the gripper over nothing without noticing.
rounds.how_found: Questioned the implicit reach assumption behind A1/A5: the candidate list only varied position and a sideways tilt, so I suspected that any place the vertical wrist cannot reach would be fatal. Screening other axes first (heavier/slippery object, other object shapes, scaled bowl/object, object on its side) showed the program already tolerated those.
rounds.why_missed: The default init states put everything in the comfortable middle of the workspace, and the earlier fixes were all about collisions, so I equated 'refused' with 'collision' and never considered kinematic reach.
rounds.fix: Added grasp candidates whose approach leans forward, away from the robot base, by 0.25/0.45/0.65 rad about the finger-closing axis (with a slightly higher grip-height range); failure retreats go to an absolute safe height instead of a relative lift; the carry retries through a high mid-waypoint if a move is refused/stopped; holding is re-checked before descent and release, and a lost object is picked up again (up to 3 pick-place cycles).
rounds.general_rule: When every motion to a target is refused, distinguish unreachable (kinematics) from blocked (collision) and answer reach failures with a different approach direction leaning away from the base, not with scene changes; and make retry motions absolute so repeated attempts cannot drift out of the workspace.

rounds.weakness: The program assumed the container is empty: it released the object over the container centre, where it came to rest on a block already inside the bowl (block top level with the rim) without touching the bowl, so the 'on/in' contact check failed every time.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A16 (nothing is already in or on the place target). Real containers are often partly filled, and the release step never looked at what is inside.
rounds.why_missed: Place targets were treated as a point (the container centre) rather than as free space inside the container; the base scene's bowl is always empty.
rounds.fix: Six repair iterations, best 0.4 (base and earlier variations stayed >= 0.9): (1) detect occupants inside the container footprint and try to take them out first - impossible with this API, because open_gripper() always opens to 8 cm and the open fingers hit the bowl rim around a 5 cm block (no partial-width opening); (2-3) release off-centre on the free side - the object still rested flat on the block top, which is above the rim; (4-5) tilt the hand 0.5/0.9 rad about the closing axis so the free end dips into the gap between block and wall - works in some seeds; (6) choose the free side away from the robot and fall back to the other side when the release pose is refused - still 0.3-0.4. Marked unsolved and the pipeline reverted to the round-3 version.
rounds.general_rule: Before releasing into a container, perceive what is already inside and plan the release into the actual free volume (or clear it first); check that your gripper can physically fit the clearing grasp (opening width vs. container wall) before relying on it.

rounds.weakness: The grasp was aimed at a single (noise-averaged) snapshot of the object. While the object slid steadily at 1.2 cm/s, the fingers closed where it had been, and grasps that did catch it were pulled out of the hand by the ongoing motion; the 5 retries ran out before the motion ended in most seeds.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7 (the object is static between detection and closing). Round 2 had shown the target can move; the object being grasped can move just as well (tray, conveyor, a person nudging it), and the retry loop only succeeded by luck once the motion stopped.
rounds.why_missed: Averaging 8 detections made a moving object look like a precise static one: averaging removes noise but hides motion, and I never looked at detections over time.
rounds.fix: Before every grasp attempt, track the object for 2 s (arm still), fit its planar velocity by least squares (resolves ~3 mm/s despite 1 cm noise) and wait in 2 s steps (up to 60 s) until it is below 6 mm/s, then grasp.
rounds.general_rule: Before acting on an object, estimate its velocity from a short time series of detections (not from a single or averaged snapshot) and wait for it to settle or predict its motion; averaging repeated detections removes noise but silently hides motion.

rounds.weakness: The object was carried and released in the hand yaw used for the grasp. With a tall post 1.2 cm beside the container, in line with the hand's wide finger-closing axis, the move above the container and the descent were refused; the program ignored the refusal and opened the gripper wherever the hand had stopped (a waypoint beside the bowl), dropping the object on the table.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9 (free space around the place target for the hand). Round 1 had shown that the hand is ~20 cm wide along the closing axis, but that lesson was only applied to the grasp, not to the release.
rounds.why_missed: I treated the place step as 'move the grip point above the target', with orientation copied from the grasp, and I did not check the result of the descent before the irreversible release.
rounds.fix: place_in_container() now tries hand yaws (0, 90, +45, -45 deg about the vertical, the object is symmetric under these for a drop) when the move above the container or the descent is refused, and never releases after a refused descent; as a last resort it returns over the container before releasing.
rounds.general_rule: Before any irreversible action, check that the preceding approach motion actually succeeded; when an approach is refused, search the free degrees of freedom of the end-effector (e.g. yaw about the approach axis) instead of acting from wherever the arm stopped.

tasks.goal: put the wine bottle on the rack

rounds.weakness: The placement was written in world axes: the wrist always pitched about world y and the bottle bottom was offset along world +x, because in the nominal scene the rack's shelf happens to run along x. With the rack turned 90 deg the bottle was laid across the shelf instead of along it and fell off every time.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (shelf runs along world x). Fixtures are moved and rotated in real kitchens far more often than their geometry changes, and the pipeline read the rack's pose only for its position, never for its orientation.
rounds.why_missed: I derived the target orientation by looking at the nominal geometry once (rack geoms, region frame) and then hard-coded what I saw as world-frame constants; only translations were taken from perception.
rounds.fix: Read the rack's region frame first and derive everything from it: the shelf axis (region x, projected horizontal) sets the finger-closing axis of the neck grasp (horizontal, perpendicular to the shelf axis), the wrist-pitch axis and the bottom offset; both bottle directions along the shelf are tried, hand on the robot side first; both gripper yaw signs are tried for the pre-grasp; the gripper never releases unless the release pose was actually reached.
rounds.general_rule: Express every target orientation and offset in the frame of the perceived goal object (its axes, not just its position), and never in world axes that only coincide with it in the nominal scene.

rounds.weakness: The grasp assumed the bottle stands upright: it went straight down to 'top of the bounding box minus 3 cm' and assumed the in-hand bottle axis equals the gripper approach axis. With the bottle lying on its side the fingers closed along the bottle axis on nothing (or on its side) and the 60 deg wrist pitch that was meant to lay it down made no sense.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A2: the pipeline read the bottle's detected orientation only to find the bounding-box top, never to decide how to grasp. Tipped-over bottles are common in real scenes.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal scene only ever showed an upright bottle, so I wrote one grasp for one pose class and treated the detected rotation as noise instead of as information that selects the strategy.
rounds.fix: Classify the detected bottle axis (upright vs lying). Lying: top grasp across the body at axis height, fingers closing perpendicular to the detected axis, several grasp points along the body and +-15 deg yaw tried when the fingers would hit a neighbour; lift, turn to the placing orientation at a safe height, lay it on the shelf with the approach along the shelf normal. The in-hand bottle axis is measured after lifting and mapped onto the shelf axis. Added a retry loop that re-detects the object after a failed or lost grasp and checks gripper_holding after lifting and before releasing.
rounds.general_rule: Use the perceived orientation of the object to choose the grasp and the in-hand-to-goal transform, with one branch per stable pose class the object can be in, instead of assuming the nominal pose class.

rounds.weakness: The neck grasp used exactly one finger-closing direction, the one the later placing motion needs (perpendicular to the shelf axis). A tall box standing 4 cm beside the bottle sat in the path of one open finger, the planner refused the descent for both yaw signs, and the pipeline had no other grasp, so it gave up on every seed.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5 (free space around the neck). The grasp yaw was chosen for the convenience of the place step, not checked against the surroundings, and real tables are cluttered.
rounds.why_missed: I coupled two decisions that are independent for a bottle held by the neck: how to grasp (constrained by clutter) and how the hand must be oriented at release (constrained by the goal). In the nominal scene the convenient yaw happened to be free.
rounds.fix: The neck grasp now tries a list of closing directions (0, 90, +-45, +-135 deg from the preferred one, both wrist signs) and takes the first the planner accepts; once the bottle hangs free in the air the wrist is turned about the vertical to the closing direction the placement needs (rotationally symmetric object about the approach axis), holding is re-checked, and the in-hand offset is measured after the turn.
rounds.general_rule: Choose the grasp from what the surroundings allow, using a set of alternatives, and fix up the orientation the goal needs afterwards in free space (re-grasp or in-air rotation), instead of forcing the goal-convenient grasp in clutter.

rounds.weakness: With the rack 10 cm closer to the robot the single release pose (bottom 3 cm along the shelf, 60 deg tilt) sat at the edge of the arm's reach: the pre-place pose was reachable but the straight descent had no IK, the joint-space fallback 'descent' swung the held bottle through the scene, and the pipeline then opened the gripper wherever the hand had stopped, dropping the bottle off the rack or leaving it perched.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9 (rack placed where the one fixed hand pose is comfortable). Fixtures are rarely exactly where they were during development, and the pipeline had exactly one release pose with no reachability alternatives.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the chosen pose was comfortably reachable, so I never saw that the goal region allows a whole family of release poses, nor that my fallbacks (joint-space descent, release regardless of where the hand ended) could do harm.
rounds.fix: A list of release-pose candidates inside the goal region (bottom offset 6/8/3 cm along the shelf, tilt 60/50 deg), tried in order; only straight-line descents (several pre-place distances), never a joint-space path for the final approach; the gripper is opened only if the hand reached within 2 cm of the planned release pose, otherwise it backs off and tries the next candidate. Also added a settling press: after release the closed fingertips press the lying bottle's body onto the shelf so it seats flat instead of staying perched on an edge.
rounds.general_rule: Treat the goal as a region and keep several reachable release poses inside it, and never execute an irreversible action (release, drop) unless the robot verifiably reached the pose that action was planned for.

rounds.weakness: Every grasp of an upright bottle came from straight above (the neck grasp, whatever its yaw). With a board 3.5 cm above the bottle top no top-down pre-grasp exists, so all yaw alternatives were refused and the pipeline gave up on every seed.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5 again, now for the vertical: the round-3 fix added alternative yaws but all of them still assumed free space above the object. Objects under shelves and overhangs are common.
rounds.why_missed: The round-3 alternatives varied only a parameter of one grasp family; I did not ask what happens when the whole family's approach corridor is blocked.
rounds.fix: Added a second grasp family for the upright bottle: a near-horizontal side grasp of the body (several azimuths and small downward pitches), followed by a short lift and a horizontal slide-out with the bottle before lifting it clear; the bottle is then held across its body and placed with the existing lying-bottle placement (in-hand axis measured, mapped onto the shelf axis, approach along the shelf normal).
rounds.general_rule: Keep alternatives across grasp families with different approach corridors (from above, from the side), not just parameter variations of one family, and plan the extraction path out of a confined grasp before lifting.

rounds.weakness: The program had exactly one way to make contact with the knob (a top-down pinch at a fixed yaw). A tall box standing 6 cm beside the knob, inside the ~20 cm footprint of the hand along its closing axis, made the planner refuse that approach on every seed. The program also did not notice the refusal: the gripper was still open (width 0.08), only a fully closed gripper counted as a miss, so it went on to 'twist' empty air about a stale axis and retried the same refused grasp three times.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A6 (nothing is beside the fin within the hand's footprint). Stove knobs on real counters sit next to bottles, pans and spice jars, and the pinch needs room for the whole hand body, not just the fingertips, so clutter near the knob was the most likely real-world violation.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the knob area was empty, so the first strategy worked on 10/10 seeds and I never checked what grasp() returns when the approach is refused, nor how much space the hand body needs compared with the part it grasps.
rounds.fix: (1) Treat a refused/incomplete approach or a gripper that is still fully open as a failed pinch. (2) Own pinch routine that tries a top-down approach and hand rolls of +-0.35/0.6 rad about the fin axis. (3) If no pinch is feasible, find movable objects whose box comes within 13 cm of the knob and relocate them: top grasp first, then side grasp, then push them away with closed fingers; set them down 15 cm further from the knob in the first direction the planner accepts. (4) Kept a tangential fingertip push of the fin as a last resort (weak in practice). Tried and rejected: pushing the fin tangentially (lever arm too short for the heavy damped knob) and tilted pinches alone (hand body still hits the box).
rounds.general_rule: Check every primitive's outcome (refused, incomplete, or a gripper that did not close) before acting on it, and when the workspace around a target is cluttered, plan for the space the whole hand needs and clear movable clutter before falling back to weaker contact strategies.

rounds.weakness: Every contact strategy assumed free space above the part: the pinch came from (nearly) straight above and the wrist twist swings the whole hand about the knob axis. With a fixed shelf 12 cm above the knob, top-down pinches are refused; steeply pitched pinches reach the fin but every twist step is refused or force-limited by the shelf. The clutter routine also wasted its time trying to grasp and push the fixed shelf (gripper_holding is true on a fixed object).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5/A16 (free space above the knob). Stove knobs often sit under range hoods, wall cabinets or pot handles, and the hand plus wrist need ~20 cm of vertical room for a top-down pinch.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal scene has open space above the knob, and I had only checked that the target pose of the pinch was feasible, not the room needed for the motion that follows it (the twist).
rounds.fix: Six repair iterations, not enough: (1) pinch orientations enumerated over pitch/roll and two approach distances, capped at 4 moving candidates; (2) a new fallback that pushes the tall end of the fin tangentially with closed fingertips from a near-horizontal hand, along the approach axis, re-seating from a fresh detection whenever the knob stops following; (3) twist and push loops stop after repeated refusal/no progress to save the 150 s step budget; (4) clutter excludes objects hanging above the knob. Push alone turns the knob on 7/10 seeds, but in the full pipeline seat attempts that move to a pre-pose and are then refused burn the step budget (6/10 StepLimitExceeded). Variation marked unsolved and reverted; the general improvements are kept (base 1.0, v1 1.0).
rounds.general_rule: Check feasibility of the whole manipulation (approach, the actuating motion and the retreat) in the actual free space before committing to a contact, and budget time: try cheap-to-refuse options first, cap expensive retries, and keep a non-grasping strategy (push or nudge) that needs less clearance.

tasks.goal: lift the peg lying on the table to an upright pose

rounds.weakness: The program released the object exactly where it had picked it up and never told the planner about other objects. With a low wall between the robot and the object, the horizontal hand and forearm needed for the upright release collided with the wall, knocking the object away (6/10 failures). A second, latent weakness surfaced while repairing: the object pivoted in the fingers during the reorienting swing, so the hand-to-object transform measured before the swing was stale at release.
rounds.how_found: Listed every motion and asked what volume it sweeps. The release pose puts the hand and forearm horizontally beside the object, a volume that is never checked, and the release spot was copied from the pick spot as if free space there were guaranteed. Clutter between a robot and its target is common on real tables. (Moving the object far forward or sideways, the first idea, did not break the program: reach was not the weak point.)
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene the table is empty, so every pose the planner could reach was also collision-free; the program was written for the empty scene and the success rate gave no signal that the free-space assumption existed.
rounds.fix: Read get_obstacles() at the start and pass every non-target object as avoid= to every move_to; raise the transport height above the tallest obstacle; choose the release spot from a ranked set of nearby candidates whose footprint is clear and let the obstacle-aware planner reject the ones where the arm does not fit; retreat upward if backing out is blocked. Re-measure the held object's pose in the hand after the swing and correct the hand pose before the final release.
rounds.general_rule: Plan every motion, including the place/release pose and the retreat, against the obstacles you perceive, and treat the place location as a choice to be checked for free space for the whole arm rather than assuming the pick location is free.

rounds.weakness: The program had exactly one grasp point (a fixed offset along the object). A second object standing 1 cm beside the object at that point left no room for a finger, so the obstacle-aware planner (correctly) refused the grasp on every attempt and the program gave up (0/10), even though most of the object's length was free.
rounds.how_found: After round 1 the program passed obstacles to the planner, so I asked what it would do when the planner says no: every fallback (retry) re-tried the same grasp point. Before choosing this, motion (sliding peg up to ~11 cm/s), mass/friction (2-3 kg, mu 0.1-0.5) and yaw (45/90 deg) were screened and did not break it (0.6-1.0), because the retry loop and the across-the-object grasp already tolerated them.
rounds.why_missed: On an empty table any grasp point works, so a single hard-coded offset never failed; the round-1 obstacle fix only added a check (planner rejection) without adding alternatives to fall back on.
rounds.fix: Generate several grasp points along the object's long axis, prefilter each by checking that both open fingers' volumes are clear of the (averaged) obstacle boxes, and take the first that the obstacle-aware planner can reach; decide which end goes up after the grasp from reachability (hand pointing away from the robot, hand above the object's centre) instead of from which half was grasped; average 20 obstacle readings instead of using one noisy reading.
rounds.general_rule: Every collision check you add must come with a set of alternatives (grasp points, approach directions, place spots) to try when it rejects the default, and the grasp must be chosen by checking that the gripper's own volume (open fingers) fits next to the object's neighbours.

rounds.weakness: The program assumed unlimited headroom: it lifted to 'above every obstacle top', used a vertical hand whose wrist needs ~0.3 m above the grasp, never checked whether a motion actually arrived, and ignored the held/standing object in planning. Under a shelf 0.39 m above the table the arm started pressed against the shelf (every plan refused), the vertical grasp did not fit, the lift sent the held peg into the shelf, pitched grasps stalled on contact and then closed anyway, and retreats routed around the shelf swept through the standing peg.
rounds.how_found: After rounds 1-2 the program reasoned about obstacles beside the object; I asked what it assumed above it. The lift height rule 'max(obstacle tops) + margin' only makes sense when nothing hangs overhead.
rounds.why_missed: Every earlier scene had open space above, so 'go higher to be safe' was always right; the planner hides collisions of anything it is not told about (the held object, the placed object) and returns success for plans that contact stops short.
rounds.fix: Kept (they do not hurt other scenes): escape move when the start state is in contact; vertical corridor (floor/ceiling) from obstacles near the object; lift heights tried from high to low under the ceiling; pitched hand approaches (60/45 deg) as alternatives to the vertical one with depth reduced so the palm clears the object; check the TCP actually reached the grasp pose before closing; release spots searched up to 0.3 m towards the robot; retreat planned with the placed object as an obstacle. Not enough: 0.1 -> 0.6. Remaining failures are random: the RRT fallback often finds long detours under the shelf, and the peg (invisible to the planner while held) is sometimes flung or snagged during the swing.
rounds.general_rule: Derive clearance from the actual free space in every direction (including overhead) instead of 'higher is safer', and never trust a planner's success for things it does not model: verify that each motion arrived, and treat held and just-placed objects as obstacles you must account for yourself.

rounds.weakness: The program looked at the scene once per attempt and then executed open-loop: the release spot was chosen before the long swing and never re-checked, so a box that slid into the work area during the swing ended up under the peg, and the peg was stood on top of the box (9/10 failures). Repairs also exposed that hovering only ~1 cm above possible obstacles let a moving object hit the held peg, and that a retreat planned with the standing peg in the avoid list started inside its inflated box and made the planner detour through it.
rounds.how_found: After round 3 the program reasoned carefully about static obstacles, so I asked how old that information was by the time it acted: obstacles were read at the start of the attempt, about 10 s before the release. In a shared workspace (people, other robots, conveyors) the scene changes in that time.
rounds.why_missed: In every earlier scene the world was static apart from the robot, so perceiving once per attempt was indistinguishable from perceiving before every step.
rounds.fix: Re-read obstacles right before committing to the release; if anything moved more than 2 cm since the attempt started, hold still until it comes to rest; if the release spot is now occupied, carry the peg at a height where its bottom clears every obstacle top to the nearest free spot. Hover 10 cm above the table (instead of 3-6 cm) until that final check, then descend. Retreat: a short straight back-off without the peg in avoid (fingers slide off it), then further moves with the peg as an obstacle; if the back-off is refused, stay put.
rounds.general_rule: Perceive again immediately before every irreversible or contact-making step (grasp, release, insertion) and compare with what you planned on; if something moved, wait for it to settle and replan, and keep held objects well clear of surfaces until that final check.

rounds.weakness: Every grasp the program knew straddled the object with open fingers. With the object lying 1 cm from a low wall along its whole length, no grasp point had room for a finger, the program correctly rejected them all and then simply gave up (0/10), although the object could easily have been slid along the wall to where a grasp fits. The oracle also scored 0/10.
rounds.how_found: After round 2 the program had alternatives for where to grasp, so I asked what it does when every alternative is rejected: it returns 'unreachable'. All its alternatives assumed the object stays where it is. Objects pressed against bin walls, tray rims or other objects are common in real clutter. Heavy, slippery, rolled, leaning and near/far objects were screened first and did not break it (0.6-1.0); only masses above a real arm's payload did.
rounds.why_missed: On an open table some grasp always fits, and the round-2 fix only added more grasps of the same kind, all on the object as it lies. Changing the object's situation before grasping was never part of the plan.
rounds.fix: If no grasp fits anywhere along the object, predict how far it must be pushed along its own axis (in each direction, checking that its path is clear and it stays in reach) until a grasp would fit, preferring pushes towards the robot. Push it with the closed fingers against an end face: try a few start gaps and heights and let the obstacle-aware planner reject those where the palm hits the wall; plan the push without the object (the planner must not avoid what it is pushing), push 4 cm past the predicted minimum to absorb the contact gap, then retreat, look again and count the push only if the object actually moved; then grasp as usual (up to 3 pushes per run).
rounds.general_rule: When no grasp fits the object where it lies, do not give up: change its situation with a non-prehensile action (push or slide it through free space to where a grasp fits), predicted from the perceived free space and confirmed by looking again afterwards.

rounds.weakness: The free-space check for the open fingers swept a volume from the table (z = 0) up, i.e. it silently assumed the object rests on the table. With the object lying on a 4 cm platform, the platform itself filled that volume at every grasp point, so every grasp was rejected and the program gave up at once (0/10), although the fingers never come near the platform. The release search also only looked within 0.30 m, too close to leave a large support.
rounds.how_found: Read every geometric check and asked which numbers are world constants rather than measured: the finger box's lower bound was a hard-coded 0.0. Objects on real robots are often picked from boxes, shelves or pallets rather than from the surface the task ends on.
rounds.why_missed: Every earlier scene had the object on the table, so 'down to the table' and 'down to the object's bottom' were the same number; the check was written in world coordinates instead of relative to the object.
rounds.fix: Sweep the finger volume from the object's perceived bottom face up (not from z = 0), and search release spots in a wider area (up to 0.40 m back and 0.35 m to the sides) so a spot beside a large support is found.
rounds.general_rule: Express every geometric check relative to what you perceive (the object's own extent and the surface it actually rests on), never relative to a hard-coded world height or reference surface, or a scene that differs only in that reference will make the check reject everything.

tasks.goal: insert the peg into the hole from the side

rounds.weakness: The pipeline averaged the peg pose once at t=0 and then executed the whole pre-grasp/grasp sequence open-loop on that estimate; when the peg slid a few cm sideways after detection, the fingers closed on empty space or on the peg's edge and nothing checked or retried (9/10 failures).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3 (the peg is static between detection and finger closure). A single detection followed by ~4 s of arm motion is a long open-loop window, and on a real table objects get bumped, roll or settle after being placed.
rounds.why_missed: All Phase 1 effort went into perception noise (averaging) and arm tracking error at the hole; in the default task nothing moves, so the grasp never failed and the stale-estimate window was invisible. Averaging many detections also hides motion: it gives a confident estimate of where the object was.
rounds.fix: Added wait_static (two averaged estimates 0.25 s apart must agree within 4 mm), re-measure the peg at the pre-grasp pose and re-plan if it moved more than 5 mm, and retry the whole grasp (up to 3 times) if gripper_holding() is false after the lift.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive the target immediately before every contact action, require it to be stationary across two estimates separated in time, and verify the result of the action (e.g. holding) with a retry loop instead of trusting an estimate taken before the arm started moving.

rounds.weakness: With a heavy (2 kg), slippery (friction 0.15) peg the single top-down grasp near the tail cannot hold it: gravity torque about the fingers makes the peg pivot until its head hits the table or jams on the rim, and the loaded arm sags and overshoots 2-3 cm at the start of every move. Grasping close to the centre of mass holds it level (v4 reached 0.8), but then the hand collides with the box face about 2 cm before the head is deep enough, which broke the default scene (base 0.2-0.7). No single grasp point satisfies both constraints.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7 (a tail grasp holds the peg rigidly): the grasp is far from the centre of mass and the fingers rely on friction only, so mass and friction directly set whether the peg rotates in the hand. A moderate change (v3, 1 kg) did not break it, the stronger one did.
rounds.why_missed: Phase 1 chose the grasp point only from the geometric clearance needed at the end of insertion (A11), with a light, grippy object where the grasp location does not matter for holding. The two requirements on the grasp point, holding against gravity torque during transport and clearance from the target at the end of the task, were never written down together, so their conflict was invisible.
rounds.fix: Not recovered within 6 repairs (pipeline reverted to round 1). Tried: grasp 3 cm behind the centre + stepwise realignment + jam detection/back-off + pushing the tail with closed fingers when the grip slips (v4 0.8 but base 0.2-0.7 because the hand hit the box face at -2 cm); grasp 4.5 cm behind the centre to clear the face (v4 dropped to 0.1). The likely solution, not tested in budget: insert partway with the centre grasp until the hole supports the peg, release, regrasp (or push) at the tail, and finish the insertion.
rounds.general_rule: When one grasp must serve both transport and final placement, derive the grasp point from both constraints (torque from the object's centre of mass during transport, and hand clearance from the target at the end), and when they conflict plan a regrasp or hand-off part-way instead of tuning a single compromise grasp point.

rounds.weakness: The grasp point was a fixed function of the object's own geometry (a set distance behind its centre), and every move_to was planned without any scene obstacles. With an immovable block 1-2 cm beside the rear half of the peg, the open finger and the hand body came down on the block every time (10/10 failures), and nothing checked whether the hand fits there or offered an alternative.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5/A6 (the space around the grasp point is free). The grasp was planned only from the target's pose, never from the scene; the hand is much wider (open fingers, palm) than the object it grasps, so anything within a few cm of it is a collision. A loose box at the same spot (v5) was pushed aside and did not break it, so the variation had to be immovable.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene the only other object (the box with the hole) is far from the peg, so collision-free grasping came for free and the hand's footprint was never modelled. The pipeline even had the obstacle list available from perception but never used it.
rounds.fix: Average the obstacle boxes of all non-task objects; model the open hand as three boxes (two fingers, palm) in the grasp frame and reject grasp candidates whose hand boxes come within 1 cm of an obstacle; try tail grasp offsets in order of preference; if none is free, pick the object up wherever the hand fits, set it down 10 cm to the side away from the obstacles, release, and grasp again normally; plan transit moves with avoid=<obstacles>. Recovered in 1 repair: v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a grasp, check the whole hand's footprint (open fingers and palm, not just the contact point) against every perceived object, search over alternative grasps when it collides, and if the task-preferred grasp is blocked, first move the object to free space with any grasp that fits and then regrasp it.

rounds.weakness: The grasp was planned purely from the object's pose, assuming the arm can comfortably reach anywhere the object might be. With the peg ~0.82 m from the robot base (inside the valid workspace, near the reach limit), the top-down pre-grasp above the tail was either unreachable (the program gave up after three identical attempts) or reached only through a long RRT detour, after which the 8 cm straight descent from that awkward configuration consumed the whole 2000-step budget.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A8: the program never considered where the robot is. The task randomises object positions over a small patch near the workspace centre, so reach margins were never exercised, while on a real table objects end up wherever the last user left them.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scenes every grasp was well inside the workspace, so move_to always succeeded quickly and reachability looked binary and free. A motion planner that reports success says nothing about how long or how well-conditioned the motion is: 'reachable' at the boundary still fails in practice.
rounds.fix: (1) If the preferred grasp point is farther than a comfortable reach (0.75 m, from the robot model; the arm's limit is ~0.85 m) from the robot base, or if its pre-grasp or grasp cannot be reached, first pick the peg at the graspable point nearest the workspace centre, carry it 15 cm inward, put it down and release; then grasp it normally. (2) Try only a few nearby grasp candidates instead of letting the planner find far-fetched detours. Recovered in 4 repairs: v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Check every planned grasp against the robot's comfortable workspace (a margin inside its reach limit, not just planner success), and when the object lies outside it, first move the object toward the workspace centre with whatever grasp is easiest, then do the task grasp from there; never accept a motion the planner only finds by a long detour.

rounds.weakness: With a shelf 15 cm above the rear half of the peg, the tail grasp itself fits under it but the wrist and forearm above a top-down hand do not, so the planner (avoiding the shelf) rejected the pre-grasp; the round-3 recovery then set the peg aside 10 cm sideways, which left it under the 30 cm-wide shelf, and repeated that until the attempts ran out.
rounds.how_found: Questioned the round-3 fix itself: its hand model stopped at the palm, and the set-aside destination was chosen by distance from the obstacle's centre, never by checking that the follow-up grasp would be free there. A large, overhanging obstacle defeats both.
rounds.why_missed: The round-3 rule was implemented only for the case that broke it (a small block beside the fingers): the footprint covered what touched that block, and 'move to free space' was approximated by 'move away from the centre', which works only for small obstacles.
rounds.fix: Added the wrist/forearm column above the hand to the footprint model, and choose the put-down spot among candidate shifts (toward the workspace centre, sideways, along the object) by checking that the object fits there (including the fixture) and that the follow-up grasp is free and comfortably reachable. Recovered in 1 repair: v11 0.9, v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Same as the obstacle rule of an earlier round: check the whole arm-and-hand footprint for the grasp, and when relocating an object, verify the precondition of the next action (a free, reachable grasp) at the destination before choosing it.

rounds.weakness: The grasp was computed from the peg's axis projected onto the table and placed at the height of the peg's centre, i.e. it assumed the object lies flat. With the peg leaning ~25 deg on a block, the grasp point near the low tail was 2-3 cm above the real axis and the hand was not square to it, so the fingers closed on the upper edge or missed (7/10 failures).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the peg lies flat). The code literally zeroed the vertical component of the measured axis and reused the centre's height, discarding information perception already provided; objects on a real table often lean on something. An 18 deg lean (v12) still mostly worked (0.5), so the tilt was increased.
rounds.why_missed: Every default scene places the peg flat on the table, so projecting the axis and reusing the centre height was exact; the simplification was invisible because it was never wrong in the scenes tested.
rounds.fix: Place the grasp point on the measured 3D axis (centre minus offset along the true axis, so its height follows the tilt) and orient the hand square to that axis: approach = straight down made perpendicular to the axis, closing = approach x axis. Identical to before for a flat peg; the in-hand servo already corrects the remaining tilt before insertion. Recovered in 1 repair: v13 0.9, v11 0.8, v9 0.9, v6 1.0, v2 1.0, base 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Plan grasps from the object's full measured 6-DoF pose, never from a projection that assumes its usual resting orientation, so the grasp point lies on the object's real geometry and the hand is square to it.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline perceived the sphere once at t=0 and then executed an open-loop grasp; a sphere that started rolling at 4 cm/s was ~10 cm away by the time the fingers arrived, so every grasp closed on air.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the object stays where it was perceived). A sphere is the object most likely to move on its own, and the pipeline had no perception between the initial detection and the grasp.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal task the sphere is always at rest, so a single (well-averaged) snapshot was enough and nothing in s0 rewarded re-checking. I averaged away perception noise but treated the scene as static, conflating 'precise' with 'current'.
rounds.fix: Estimate velocity from a time series of averaged detections (line fit, 1 s) before every attempt; if moving, go to a meeting point ahead on the path sized by speed x expected arm time, re-measure there (heading from the long baseline between the two measurements), lower the open fingers across the path, close when the object is predicted to reach the TCP mid-close; verify gripper_holding() and retry. Debugging also showed that re-orienting the wrist during the descent made the planner 5x slower, letting the object pass.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive an object immediately before every contact and estimate its velocity, not just its position; if it moves, plan to where it will be after your own motion time and verify the grasp before continuing.

rounds.weakness: Every motion was planned with no collision objects and the carry height was a constant (z=0.12), so a 15 cm wall between pick and place was hit by the arm and the held sphere. After obstacles were given to the planner, a second weakness appeared: the wrist yaw was fixed (45 deg), and with it the 20 cm-wide hand came within the planner's safety margin of the wall both at the pick and over the bin, so move_to was refused, and the pipeline ignored the refusal and closed the gripper on air.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A2 (the straight paths between waypoints are free). The pipeline never called get_obstacles() or used avoid, so any object between pick and place would be invisible to it.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal table is empty, so open-space screw motions always worked and the planner's collision checking was never exercised. I also treated the gripper as a point at the TCP and ignored the hand's footprint, which depends on the wrist yaw.
rounds.fix: Pass every non-task object to the planner on every motion; compute the carry height from the detected obstacle tops plus the held object's size (the planner does not model the object in the hand); move as lift, then horizontal transit, then descend. Try a ranked list of wrist yaws (diagonal to the bin first, then along the walls) at the pick and over the place, keeping the first one the planner accepts, and release slightly higher when the fingers are along the walls. Check every move_to return value before acting on it.
rounds.general_rule: Give the planner every known obstacle, inflate for the object you are carrying (which the planner does not see), treat the hand's footprint and orientation as free variables to search over, and check every motion's return value before the next action.

rounds.weakness: The round-2 fix computed one carry height as 'above the highest obstacle'. With a shelf over the bin, that height put the hand above the shelf, and every descent into the bin was blocked. Underneath it was a second weakness: the hand was always vertical (top-down), and a probe showed the arm cannot reach any point under a 30 cm overhang with a vertical hand, even with the shelf removed from the planner. A forward tilt of 0.6-0.9 rad reaches all of them.
rounds.how_found: Questioned B4 (obstacles only matter by their top). The carry height was derived from max(top) alone, which treats every obstacle as a floor and never as a ceiling.
rounds.why_missed: The round-2 obstacle was a wall, and for a wall 'go higher' is always correct, so the fix generalised the instance instead of the geometry. The vertical hand had never been questioned because every earlier target was in open space.
rounds.fix: Candidate carry heights are the lowest safe height plus each obstacle top + clearance. A height is kept only if the held object clears every obstacle over the pick-place corridor in z, from both below and above. Heights are tried lowest first, and at each height the pipeline searches hand tilt (0, 0.6, 0.9 rad forward) x wrist yaw, taking the first transfer and descent the planner accepts. It releases slightly higher when the hand is tilted or the fingers are along the walls.
rounds.general_rule: Free space is bounded from above as well as below: choose the lowest motion that keeps the carried object clear in every direction, and when a target is unreachable, search the hand's full orientation (tilt as well as yaw) before concluding it is blocked.

rounds.weakness: The grasp height was a constant (sphere radius above z=0, i.e. 'the object rests on the table'), while x and y came from perception. With the sphere on a 12 cm platform, the pre-grasp pose was inside the platform and the grasp pose 12 cm below the sphere. The planner refused every one of them, and the pipeline retried the same impossible poses until it gave up.
rounds.how_found: Questioned B5. The pipeline used the measured x and y of the object but threw away the measured z in favour of a constant that encoded a belief about the support surface.
rounds.why_missed: On the nominal task the constant and the measurement agree to the millimetre, so the shortcut looked harmless; it was written when 'the table' was the only support surface in the scene. Earlier fixes re-measured position for motion (x, y, velocity) but never audited which coordinates were still hard-coded.
rounds.fix: All grasp and pre-grasp heights now come from the averaged measured position of the object (static and rolling grasps). The existing carry-height logic then treats the platform as an obstacle under the corridor and lifts the sphere above it.
rounds.general_rule: Derive every coordinate of a target pose from perception; any constant that encodes where an object 'normally' is (support height, orientation, size) is an untested assumption that will fail the first time the object is somewhere else.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline handled every non-task object only as an obstacle to plan around. With a block already sitting in the bin, it scored 0.0 (gate). The failing episodes were not traced; the inferred mechanism is that the block, given to the planner as an obstacle, made every descent into the bin collide, and the pipeline has no action that frees the goal.
rounds.how_found: Questioned C1 (the goal is empty). Every fix so far had made the pipeline better at avoiding things, which made it more likely to treat a blocked goal as unreachable rather than as something to change.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal bin is always empty, and the obstacle fixes of rounds 2-3 framed every other object as fixed scenery. I never asked whether the precondition of the final action (an empty target) actually held.
rounds.fix: Before picking up the sphere (while the hand is still empty), detect any non-task object inside the goal footprint, grasp it (excluding it from the planner's obstacle list for that grasp), move it to free table space beside the goal on the side away from the sphere, re-check the goal, and only then re-measure the obstacles and run the normal pick-and-place.
rounds.general_rule: Before an action, check its preconditions on the target (free, reachable, stable), and when one fails, consider changing the scene (move the blocker, while the hand is free) instead of only planning around it.

tasks.goal: plug the charger into the receptacle

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed the charger rests on its bottom face: the top grasp took the base's y axis projected on the horizontal as the closing direction, which is degenerate when the charger lies on its side, and the only in-hand pose it can insert from is the upright one. A side-lying charger needs a regrasp (roll 90 deg and put it down), and that regrasp was not made reliable within 6 repair iterations.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (orientation): the grasp code zeroes the z component of a body axis and normalizes it, which only makes sense if that axis is horizontal. Tipped-over parts are common on real tables.
rounds.why_missed: Phase 1 only saw the task's own randomization (yaw only), so every grasp computation silently relied on the object being upright, and the insertion was built around one in-hand pose.
rounds.fix: Not recovered (best 0.3 on v1, debug evals). Tried: (1) oriented-box top grasp: grasp works but the rolled in-hand pose puts the 20 cm hand vertically at receptacle height and it hits the table; (2-4) roll in the air and release: the hand cannot get low with the closing axis vertical, the part rides on the lower finger or drops 10 cm and lands upside down; (5) grasp across the part's long axis with a 45 deg approach that bisects world-down before and after the roll, then place it 2 mm above the table: lands upright in one roll on most seeds; (6) check each move's endpoint and re-plan, pitch the insertion grasp away from the receptacle. Remaining failures: the regrasp sometimes closes on nothing although move_to reported success, the part is flung when the hand re-plans while holding it, and the extra moves exhaust the 2000-step budget. Pipeline reverted to the Phase 1 version; last attempt kept in wip/pipeline_v1_repair6.py.
rounds.general_rule: When the required in-hand pose cannot be grasped directly from the object's resting pose, plan the regrasp as a place, not a drop: choose a grasp axis that stays horizontal through the reorientation and an approach that is clear of the support surface both before and after it, and verify after every grasp that the object is actually held before continuing.

rounds.weakness: The grasp was computed once from the detections taken at t=0 and executed open loop. The charger was pushed ~26 mm just as the hand arrived, so the fingers closed on the moving part: it slid in the grip and was held at its peg end, and the fingers then struck the receptacle face 16 mm before full insertion (0.4).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3: the only perception before contact happened at the start of the episode, and nothing re-checks the object before the gripper closes. Objects on a real table get bumped or settle.
rounds.why_missed: In the base task nothing moves, so one (very well averaged) measurement was always valid; accuracy was optimised, freshness was never considered. The pipeline also treated 'gripper is holding something' as success of the grasp, though the insertion depends on where in the hand the part sits.
rounds.fix: At the pre-grasp pose, wait until two averaged estimates 0.25 s apart agree (object at rest), compare with the pose the grasp was planned from, and re-plan the grasp if it moved more than 3 mm. After closing: require gripper_holding, and after lifting compare the measured in-hand pose with the planned one; if it is more than 8 mm off, put the part down and regrasp. Recovered 1.0 on base and v2.
rounds.general_rule: Re-observe the target immediately before committing to contact and only act on a measurement taken while it is at rest; after grasping, check that the object sits in the hand where the plan assumed, not merely that something is held.

rounds.weakness: Every free-space move was a straight screw motion planned for the bare arm against an empty world: after lifting the charger 5 cm the pipeline moved straight to the pre-insertion pose, dragging the charger and fingers through a 9 cm wall between the pick and place areas (0.0; the official oracle also scored 0.0).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7: no move_to call passed avoid=, and the lift height (5 cm) was chosen for the empty task table, not for what stands between start and goal. Real workspaces have trays, rims and other objects between pick and place locations.
rounds.why_missed: The base scene has nothing but the two task objects, so the shortest path was always free; and the planner's own collision model covers the arm only, so even an obstacle-aware call would not have protected the part hanging below the fingers.
rounds.fix: transfer(): treat every non-task object as an obstacle (averaged oriented boxes from get_obstacles), rise vertically to 5 cm above the highest obstacle top, travel at that height, then descend onto the pre-insertion pose, all with avoid=; the pre-grasp move also avoids non-task objects. Also found while repairing: gripper_holding() read False right after closing on a good grasp (contact registers a few steps later), so the v2 miss-handling lifted and later dropped a held part; now it waits up to 0.5 s for the signal and opens the gripper before retreating after a real miss. Recovered 1.0 on base, v2, v3.
rounds.general_rule: Plan free-space moves for the arm plus whatever it is holding: clear obstacles by the held object's extent below the gripper (e.g. rise above the tallest obstacle, travel, then descend) instead of trusting a straight-line or arm-only collision check.

rounds.weakness: With a 0.3 kg, low-friction charger in hand the arm settled a few mm below and ~0.01 rad off its commanded pose. The servo loop removed this offset while holding still in front of the receptacle, but every new servo call started again from the uncompensated command, so the 6 mm insertion stroke brought the pegs ~3 mm low onto the receptacle face (0.0; oracle 0.0). The part did not actually slip in the fingers.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9/A10 (in-hand slip, a light grippy part); diagnosis with the true in-hand pose showed the hold constant and the error coming from the arm's load-dependent tracking offset instead.
rounds.why_missed: With the light default part the arm's steady-state error was well under the 0.5 mm clearance, so per-move feedback that restarted from the nominal command looked sufficient; the integral correction was local to one call and its learned value was thrown away.
rounds.fix: servo_to re-measures the in-hand pose after every free-space move and, when the part's orientation is off by more than 0.005 rad, shifts the full commanded pose by (last command vs pose reached); the free-space position offset (command minus reached) is stored and added to every later command, including the contact-phase insertion steps. Two earlier attempts (re-aiming to the same nominal pose; integral re-aim without carrying the offset) did not converge. Recovered 1.0 on base, v2, v3, v4.
rounds.general_rule: Treat the controller's steady-state tracking error under the current load as a calibration: measure command-versus-reached in free space just before a precision move and carry that offset into the contact moves, instead of re-commanding nominal targets after each correction.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed the part's yaw is within +-60 deg of the insertion direction. With the charger reversed (pegs toward the robot) the hand must turn it ~180 deg about the vertical between grasp and insertion, which no grasp choice avoids: on some seeds the wrist hit its joint range and the planner stopped short while reporting success, on others the insertion jammed (0.0; oracle 0.0).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A12: the grasp was chosen to minimise wrist rotation at pick time, never checking the rotation needed later at the goal. A part put down the wrong way round is common.
rounds.why_missed: The task's yaw range kept the pick-to-place rotation small, so the grasp heuristic (closing aligned with the current TCP y) was always also fine for the insertion.
rounds.fix: If the yaw error to the insertion direction exceeds 60 deg, turn the charger on the table first: pick it up 3 cm, turn it by at most 90 deg about the vertical, put it down, re-detect, repeat. Grasp candidates (both closing directions, and for turning-only grasps both lean directions) are tried until move_checked confirms the pre-grasp pose was really reached. The insertion grasp's 15 deg pitch now always leans toward the pegs so the palm stays clear of the receptacle (same finding as in v1). Recovered 1.0 on base, v2-v5 (5 repair iterations).
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a grasp, check that the whole sequence it implies (pick, carry, final pose) stays within the arm's joint range; if the required reorientation is too large, reorient the object in steps through place-and-regrasp, and verify that each motion actually reached its target instead of trusting the planner's success flag.

tasks.goal: use the tool to pull the cube within reach

rounds.weakness: The pipeline reduced the tool's detected 3D orientation to a single yaw angle and hard-coded which side of the handle the hook is on. When the tool lay flipped over (a mirror image in the table plane, yaw still ~0), it put the handle on the wrong side of the cube and lowered the hook into empty table, so the pull never touched the cube (0/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the tool lies upright, so yaw describes it). The first attempt at this round, a 180-degree yaw of the tool, was rejected by the break gate (0.9), which showed yaw was already handled; flipping is the orientation change that yaw cannot see.
rounds.why_missed: In every default episode the tool spawns upright with the same face up, so a yaw-only model of its pose was always right and the hook side looked like a constant of the task.
rounds.fix: detect_avg now returns the full rotation (chordal mean of the noisy detection rotations, projected back with SVD). The hook direction is read from the full rotation (sign of the tool's +y axis after rotating the handle to world +x), the handle is placed on the opposite side of the cube from the hook, and the hand-to-tool transform and target pose use the full rotation instead of a yaw-only quaternion.
rounds.general_rule: Derive the direction of every functional feature of an object (hook, opening, handle side) from its full detected 3D rotation, never from yaw alone or from the side it usually faces, since objects can be lying flipped or mirrored.

rounds.weakness: The cube was detected once at the very start and the hook was placed from that stale estimate about 10 s later.
