When the cube was pushed 13 cm sideways while the robot fetched the tool, the hook came down where the cube used to be and the pull dragged nothing (0/10). While repairing, a second weakness appeared on the base task: the tool, gripped near its end with the hook mass 17 cm away, pivoted up to 35 deg in the fingers during the fast carry, so the drooping hook swept the table and knocked the cube out of reach; the in-hand pose measured once after the lift was then wrong.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A8 (objects stay where they were first seen), because the target is acted on long after it is perceived and on a real table things get bumped. A first design with a 1.5 cm push was rejected by the break gate (1.0): the placement clearances absorbed it, so the push had to exceed the clearance to test the assumption.
rounds.why_missed: In the default task nothing moves, so one detection at the start was always still valid, and the initial grasp of the tool happened to hold it rigidly enough at the default speeds in the 10 evaluation seeds.
rounds.fix: Before placing the tool, hold still until two consecutive half-second windows of cube detections agree within 1.2 cm, then re-detect the cube (20 averaged detections) and plan the hook placement from that. Carry the held tool at slow speed, re-measure the tool-in-hand transform after every carry (after lift, after transfer, after lowering), and compute the hand pose so that the tool itself is level (target orientation of the tool, not of the hand).
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive every object right before the step that depends on its pose (and wait until it is still), and after picking up anything that is used to act on the world, re-measure its pose in the hand after each carry and command the held object's pose rather than the hand's.

rounds.weakness: The pull went straight back along -x with no knowledge of other objects, so an immovable block right behind the cube jammed it (0/10). The first repair also showed that the obstacle check must include the gripper itself: the 0.2 m-wide hand (along the finger axis) came down on top of the block while the handle was being lowered beside the cube, and the tool was knocked out of the fingers.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9 (the straight path from the cube to the goal is free), the assumption a cluttered real table most often violates.
rounds.why_missed: The default scene contains only the tool and the cube, so no path was ever blocked and get_obstacles() was never called.
rounds.fix: Kept for later rounds: read get_obstacles(), check the swept footprint of tool, cube AND hand (real hand box measured from the robot's collision geometry) along each candidate stroke, and choose a plan from: straight pull, sideways detour pushed by the handle then pull, and a tilted tool that raises the hand. Not recovered: with the cube 0.83 m from the base and the block directly behind it, every configuration that avoids sweeping the long handle into the block needs the hand 0.82-0.88 m from the base, beyond the arm's ~0.80 m reach at table height. Oracle also 0.0. Marked unsolved and replaced by v4 (block further back in the lane).
rounds.general_rule: Collision-check the whole swept volume of every stroke, including your own hand and the held tool, against all perceived obstacles before executing it, and verify a detour stays within the arm's reach.

rounds.weakness: Same as v3 in a solvable layout: an immovable block halfway down the straight pull lane; the round-2 pipeline pulled the cube straight into it (0/10).
rounds.how_found: v3 attacked A9 but was not solvable within reach; v4 moves the block (and the fixed cube spot) so a detour exists. It is labelled parameter_tuning because only the positions changed relative to v3.
rounds.why_missed: See v3: the default scene never blocks the lane.
rounds.fix: The obstacle-aware planner written during v3: averaged get_obstacles() boxes, swept-footprint check (tool parts, cube, hand + fingers; 7 mm margin for tool/cube, 15 mm for the hand), plans tried in order of how unusual they are (straight pull, then sideways handle push of increasing length then pull, then the same with the tool tilted to raise the hand), vertical descent also checked. Here it picks a 0.22 m sideways push and then the pull. Note: this fix was written during the v3 attempt; the v4 gate measured the committed round-2 pipeline (s_break 0.0).
rounds.general_rule: When the direct path to the goal is blocked, search over a small set of motion primitives (push sideways, then pull) and execute the cheapest sequence whose full swept footprint is collision-free.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline always lifted and carried the tool by its free end. With a tool twice as heavy (1.0 kg) the gravity torque exceeded the grip friction, the tool swung to ~45 deg in the fingers, its drooping hook knocked the cube away during the carry, and the placement computed for a level tool was wrong (0/10). The repair also exposed two latent weaknesses: contact moves that fail the straight-line planner silently fell back to RRT (which lifted the tool off the cube mid-pull), and waypoints were chosen without checking that they were within the arm's reach (one episode spent 1400 steps on an unreachable waypoint).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A10 (the held tool is rigid in the hand). A sweep showed that a heavy or high-friction cube (2 kg, mu 2) and a slippery tool did not break the pipeline, but a heavier tool did, because it is held 12 cm from its centre of mass.
rounds.why_missed: With the default 0.5 kg tool the pivot is only ~5 deg at slow speed, so lifting by the end looked safe; the reach limit and the RRT fallback never showed because the default placements happened to be reachable along straight lines.
rounds.fix: Test lift: after lifting, measure how much the tool hangs in the fingers; if more than 12 deg, put it back down and slide it on the table (the table carries its weight) to a pre-hook pose beside the cube, then sideways into the hooking pose, with the slide route checked against the cube and obstacles. All contact moves (slide, sideways push, pull) are split into 4 cm straight hops. The tool is laid and pulled along the radial direction from the robot base to the cube, and every plan and route is checked against a reach limit (0.80 m from the base).
rounds.general_rule: After grasping an object you will use as a tool, do a test lift and measure how much it slips or pivots in the grip; if it does, keep it supported (slide it) or regrasp nearer its centre of mass, and make every contact move short straight segments within verified reach.

rounds.weakness: The tool was always grasped top-down at one fixed point 2.5 cm from the handle's free end, at a hard-coded table-level height. With a 15 cm tall bottle-sized block standing right beside that end of the handle, the open fingers and the 0.2 m-wide hand came down onto the block, so the grasp failed or knocked the tool away (0/10). The oracle also failed (0.0).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3 and A4 (the tool rests on the table and its fixed grasp point is free). A first design that raised the tool on a 6 cm platform (attacking A3) was rejected by the break gate (1.0): the hand's compliance still produced a grasp at the wrong height. That showed the height was not the weak point, but the fixed grasp location was, so v6 blocks the approach to that location instead.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene nothing but the cube is near the tool, so the first grasp point was always clear and the grasp was never checked against clutter.
rounds.fix: Choose the grasp point along the handle (candidates 2.5-12.5 cm from the free end) as the first one whose vertical approach is clear: the hand box plus the open-finger box is checked against get_obstacles() (the tool itself excluded). The grasp height comes from the perceived tool pose (grip_z = tool z) and the lift height from max(0.15, tool z + 0.12). If the chosen point is not the usual one, set the tool down at a nearby free spot (footprint checked with the tool's rotation) and regrasp it at the usual point, so the rest of the program (test lift, carry or slide, hook placement) runs unchanged. Seeds 0-9: 1.0 on every scene; held-out seeds 100-119: 1.0 everywhere except v6 (0.95).
rounds.general_rule: Before grasping, check the approach of the gripper (hand and open fingers) for clutter at several candidate grasp points and take the first clear one; if that grasp is unsuitable for using the object, use it only to move the object to free space, then regrasp properly.

tasks.goal: Move the bowl to left and right by pressing the corresponding keys to catch the red ball.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline sent each arm straight to the key centre in its home gripper yaw and pressed with move_to calls that had no avoid list. An 18 cm post 1.5 cm beside the left key overlapped the 16 cm wide gripper palm: the planner (whose model does not include the gripper) still returned success, the palm jammed on the post 5 cm above the hover pose, the key never fired and the bowl could not be driven left (7 of 10 seeds lost).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A13 (free path to the key). The pipeline treated a key as a point and the gripper as having no size; real buttons sit among clutter, and the API planner only avoids what it is given (and, it turned out, not with the gripper's own geometry).
rounds.why_missed: The empty table made every straight top-down approach succeed, and move_to returning True looked like proof that the gripper got there. I never compared the reached pose with the target, and never asked how wide the tool is relative to the free space around the target.
rounds.fix: Measure the static obstacles once (get_obstacles minus the task objects) and pass them as avoid; model the gripper as a 16x9 cm footprint reaching 17 cm below the flange; choose the gripper yaw (0 or 90 deg) and press-point offset within the key's capture radius that clears every obstacle box by 1.5 cm over the whole press stroke; approach from above the tallest nearby obstacle, then descend; accept a move only if the measured pose is within 1.2 cm of the target.
rounds.general_rule: Before approaching a target, check the tool's full footprint (not just its tip) against known obstacles over the whole approach and stroke, choose an orientation or offset that clears them, and verify the reached pose instead of trusting the planner's success flag.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline never checked that the receptacle was empty. With a canister standing in the bowl it servoed the bowl under the ball, the ball bounced off the canister, and 9 of 10 seeds failed. A thinner stick (v3, rejected) slid aside or was flung out by the bowl's starts and stops, which hid the problem half the time.
rounds.how_found: Listed what the pipeline assumes about the goal region rather than about the moving objects: nothing in the code reads the bowl's contents, and on a real robot a container often still holds the last item.
rounds.why_missed: The task statement only talks about moving the bowl and catching the ball; I modelled the bowl as a target point, not as a container whose state is a precondition.
rounds.fix: Tried: before anything else, list objects whose box sits inside the bowl; take each out with a horizontal side grasp from the robot side just above the rim (a top-down grasp would hit the shelves overhead), lift 7.5 cm, back out, set it down standing between the keys, open, and pull the fingers away before any later close. Pushing it over the far rim failed (the palm rode up on the rim). The clearing works (0.4 overall), but it costs ~8 s plus 2.4 s of gripper closing with one blocking primitive at a time, and on 5 seeds the ball lands within 5.7-11.7 s, so 0.8 was out of reach. Marked unsolved after 4 repair iterations and reverted the pipeline to round 1 (attempt kept in attempts/pipeline_v4_unsolved.py).
rounds.general_rule: Check that the goal location or receptacle is actually free before relying on it, and when it must be cleared first, budget the clearing time against the deadline at the start instead of discovering the overrun afterwards.

rounds.weakness: Round 1 made the press configuration obstacle-aware but from a single snapshot taken at the start. A post that slid in next to the left key at 4-6 s (after the arms were in place) jammed the hovering gripper exactly as in v2, and the left key stopped working for the rest of the episode. (The same post arriving at 7-9 s, v6, only cost half the seeds; a block lying on the key, v5, was simply shoved off by the press.)
rounds.how_found: Read the round-1 fix as a new assumption: 'obstacles are static, measure them once'. Real workspaces change while the robot works, and nothing in the loop re-perceived them.
rounds.why_missed: The fix for round 1 was written against a static obstacle, so it inherited the original program's habit of perceiving the scene once and then acting open-loop on that snapshot, even though the main control loop already re-perceives the ball and the bowl 50 times a second.
rounds.fix: Tried: re-read the obstacles every 0.2 s (one noisy reading, re-snapshot averaged over five readings if anything moved more than 3 cm), re-plan the press configuration only when the current one no longer clears (hysteresis against sensor noise), plan against where a moving obstacle will be 0.3-1.5 s later, and use a double margin on re-plans so one re-plan suffices. It works (the arm turns away from the arriving post and presses again), but each re-plan costs 1-1.6 s of key downtime (lift, turn, descend) inside the 5-8 s window in which several seeds land; v7 stayed at 0.5-0.7 over six iterations on a noisy shared host, so it is marked unsolved and the pipeline is reverted to round 1 (attempt in attempts/pipeline_v7_unsolved.py).
rounds.general_rule: Treat every perceived fact the plan depends on, including obstacles and free space, as something that can change: re-check it inside the control loop and re-plan when it no longer holds, rather than snapshotting it once at the start.

rounds.weakness: The program only pushed the box along one axis (away from the robot) and relied on dragging it sideways with a finger in contact to fix any error along the other axis; with the box starting 0.3 m from the catch point along that other axis, the box never got past the boundary line (0/10).
rounds.how_found: Listed where the pipeline assumes objects start: the approach and push targets were computed at the box's own x and only the y error was ever re-checked, which only works if the box already starts near the landing x as in the default spawn.
rounds.why_missed: Every default seed spawns the box within 4 cm of the landing x, so a one-axis push plus friction drag passed the base task; the first draft was shaped by the default spawn rather than by the goal geometry.
rounds.fix: Measure the box's offset from the target on both axes and, when the x offset exceeds 2.5 cm, first push the box along x with one fingertip on its x face (calibrated 5.7 cm contact offset, 6 cm segments at about 0.3 m/s), back off, then do the y push as before.
rounds.general_rule: Plan a push from the full vector between where the object is and where it must go, pushing along each needed direction from the appropriate face, instead of assuming the object starts where it usually does.

rounds.weakness: The program always put the hand 15 cm behind the object in a fixed grip, never looked for other things on the table and planned no collision checks against them; a fixed block 11-14 cm behind the box sat exactly where the trailing finger had to go, so the hand jammed against it, the push never started and the episodes stalled (0/10, six seeds hit the 15 min worker timeout).
rounds.how_found: Questioned what is between the gripper and the target: the approach and push poses were computed only from the box pose, with no obstacle query and no avoid list, and the chosen grip needs a large empty strip behind the object.
rounds.why_missed: The default scene has nothing on the table but the task objects, so the free space the grip needed was never visible as a requirement; the grip was tuned for contact geometry only.
rounds.fix: Query get_obstacles() at the start; compute the free strip each grip needs behind the object and switch from the 'fingers along the push' grip (needs ~22 cm) to a 'fingers across, hand offset 6 cm to the side' grip (needs ~9 cm) when the first is blocked; pass the obstacles as avoid on free-space moves and descend straight into the narrow slot. While repairing, the base task exposed a second weakness: the first push went all the way to an early, noisy landing estimate and the late re-prediction loop was skipped when the early release-time estimate was too soon; now the first push stops at the lane centre, release time is floored at 5.3 s, and corrections creep forward in 5 cm steps until 0.45 s before release.
rounds.general_rule: Before choosing how to hold a tool or approach an object, check the free space that grasp or approach actually needs against everything perceived nearby, and keep an alternative grip with a smaller footprint for cluttered cases.

rounds.weakness: Once the box had been pushed into place the program only kept re-checking the one coordinate it was correcting (y) and could only push from the robot side; when the box was knocked 7 cm sideways two seconds before the catch it never noticed the new x error, and its fixed sequence of special-case manoeuvres (push x once, then y, an expensive go-round only for -y) could neither re-plan nor fit the remaining time (2/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned whether objects move after the robot has acted on them: the correction loop compared only dy against the target and assumed the box stays where the last push left it.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene nothing touches the box except the gripper, so a one-axis correction loop after an open-loop placement always looked sufficient; disturbances after placement were never imagined.
rounds.fix: Replaced the scripted push sequence with a closed-loop controller: every cycle it re-predicts the landing, measures the box on both axes, picks the axis to fix (x first), moves the hand over the top of the box to the right face only when needed and only if the remaining time allows, pushes, and if the box stopped short of where the hand pushed it learns that shortfall and pushes further next time. Six repair iterations: one-axis re-check (0.2), faster re-centring (0.4, 0.4), conservative early y target plus side-step push-back (0.3), general face-switching controller (0.7), learned push overshoot (0.8).
rounds.general_rule: After acting on an object, keep re-measuring every quantity the success condition depends on until the deadline, and correct with a general closed loop that can choose any approach direction, rather than a fixed script that only re-checks what it last changed.

rounds.weakness: When the box was shoved 7 cm away from the robot 1.1-2.3 s before the catch, the program could only undo it by moving the hand over the box to its far side and pushing back; that manoeuvre took 1.2-1.8 s (a 90 degree wrist turn alone cost ~0.5 s, the far side was out of reach for the default grip, and the hand had to stay out of the ball's flight corridor), so it finished after the ball left the ramp on most seeds (best 0.4 over five repairs; v3 also dropped to 0.4-0.7 while trying).
rounds.how_found: Questioned the assumption, kept after round 3, that late corrections are cheap because the hand already rests on the robot-side face; a disturbance in the other direction close to the deadline tests whether the controller can reverse in time.
rounds.why_missed: The default scene never moves the box away from the hand, and the round-3 fix was tuned on a sideways knock that a side push could undo; reversal time near the deadline was never budgeted.
rounds.fix: Tried, not kept (dev/pipeline_v4_last_attempt.py): face-dependent grips with the compact grip for the far face, reach fallback, keep-out of the flight corridor, earlier stop near the exit, home-orientation grip by default to avoid wrist turns, longer push segments. None reached 0.8 on v4 without breaking v3. Pipeline reverted to the round-3 version; v4 marked unsolved.
rounds.general_rule: Budget the worst-case time to reverse a correction against the deadline before committing to a one-sided strategy; if reversing takes longer than the time left, constrain the object on both sides (or hold it) rather than relying on pushing from one side.

rounds.weakness: The program treated every perceived obstacle as a full-height wall and always pushed with the fingertips 6 mm above the table; a 2.2 cm rail 3-9 cm behind the box made both grips look blocked, the fingers came down on the rail and the push never started (2/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned what lies under the hand rather than beside it: the push height was a constant and the free-space check ignored obstacle heights, while the contact only needs the fingertips somewhere on the 4 cm box wall.
rounds.why_missed: The table was empty in every earlier scene, and the round-2 obstacle was taller than the hand, so height never mattered; the push height was tuned once for the bare table.
rounds.fix: Average the noisy obstacle boxes over 10 looks, raise the push height just enough for the fingertips to clear low obstacles near the box (as long as they still meet the box wall below its rim), and ignore those obstacles in the free-space check. Keeping v3 at 0.8 needed a second change: each push now closes the loop on the box itself (extra short slides while the box is still short and still moving), because a box turned by a bump presents a corner and the fixed contact offset left it 2-5 cm short.
rounds.general_rule: Use the measured heights of nearby objects, not just their footprints, to pick the contact height of a push or grasp within the band the target allows, and close the loop on the object's position rather than on the hand's.

tasks.goal: Guide the ball through the target hole of the rotating sorter into the container.

rounds.weakness: The grasp aimed at one averaged snapshot of the ball's position. When the ball started rolling (4 cm/s) the gripper closed where the ball had been, and every retry re-aimed at a fresh but already stale position, closing on empty space until the ball rolled off the table (0/10). A perception call also threw once on the platform, which crashed that run.
rounds.how_found: A1 in assumptions.md: between the detection and the moment the fingers close there are 1-2 s of arm motion, and the scene is explicitly dynamic, so a still target is the first thing a real scene breaks (a nudged or rolling object).
rounds.why_missed: In the base task the ball always lay still until touched, so position-only perception was enough and the retry loop looked like robustness; the retry never checked whether the target was still where it had been aimed.
rounds.fix: acquire_ball(): estimate the ball's velocity from 6 averaged detections over 0.5 s; if it moves, pre-position the open gripper 2.6 s ahead on its path with the closing axis across the motion, then re-measure in a closed loop and close only when the ball is between the fingers (along-track distance <= speed x close delay, lateral < 3 cm); a still ball must be within 1.5 cm of the finger centre or the attempt aborts upward and retries. Also: detect() failures are caught, and the carry ends with a correcting move to the release point.
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a contact action, estimate the target's velocity (not just its position) and re-verify its pose relative to the end effector immediately before the irreversible step; intercept a moving target at a predicted point with the gripper oriented to receive it, and abort rather than act blind when the check fails.

rounds.weakness: The carry moved the held ball 8 cm above the platform top with no obstacle list and no check of the moves' results. Two walls between the ball and the sorter (top 6 cm above the carry height) knocked the ball out of the gripper or stopped the arm; when the long carry move failed to plan, the next (lower) move was executed anyway and dragged the ball through the wall (0/10).
rounds.how_found: A6 in assumptions.md: every motion passed no avoid list and the transport height was set only by the target surface, so anything taller than that between pick and place was invisible to the program; clutter on the path is the commonest real-world difference.
rounds.why_missed: The base scene had nothing between the ball and the sorter and the planner always avoided the table, so collision-free paths came for free; I also treated a failed move as harmless and carried on with the next waypoint.
rounds.fix: Perceive obstacles (get_obstacles averaged over 10 calls) and pass them to every motion; raise the carry height so the held ball's bottom clears the top of any obstacle near the pick-to-place corridor by 3.5 cm (the planner models the arm, not the held object); move the ball by its own centre (move_ball_to) and, when a plan fails, retry with the gripper turned about the vertical (a sphere's grasp yaw is free) or via a higher midpoint, and stop instead of continuing low if all fail; try every top-down grasp candidate until one whose approach and straight descent both plan.
rounds.general_rule: Size every transport waypoint to the swept volume of the arm plus the held object (the planner usually models only the arm), pass perceived obstacles to every plan, and treat a failed motion as a stop condition that triggers an alternative, never as a step to skip.

rounds.weakness: The release point was hard-coded as the point of the hole's orbit on the working arm's own side. Two brackets hanging over the sorter on both sides (3 cm thick, 7 cm above the platform) left that point unreachable at the release height; the arm stopped above the bracket and opened there, so the ball landed on the bracket or the solid platform (0/10).
rounds.how_found: A5/A13: P = centre + side * [r, 0] was a convenience choice, not a requirement; the goal only needs the ball to meet the hole, which passes under every point of its orbit once per revolution. A fixed place pose is exactly what a fixture or clamp near the goal invalidates.
rounds.why_missed: The first free choice worked, so I never wrote down that it was a choice; the set of equivalent goal poses was collapsed to one point in the code.
rounds.fix: release_point(): enumerate points of the hole's orbit (every 15 deg, starting from the arm's side and turning towards the robot first) and take the first whose vertical column (gripper radius 4.5 cm, 35 cm above the platform) is free of perceived obstacles; the timing solver already works for any orbit angle.
rounds.general_rule: When the goal admits a family of equivalent target poses (any point on a path, any angle about a symmetry axis), keep the whole family in the program and choose a member at run time by checking it against the perceived free space, instead of hard-coding the first one that worked.

rounds.weakness: Grasp orientation was whatever the candidate generator ranked first (fingers along world x). With a box 6 mm beside the ball on that axis, an open finger came down on the box: the ball was pushed or the arm stopped, and the 'still, off-centre' check then retried into the same collision (s_break 0.3). After the fix forced the fingers along y, a second, hidden weakness appeared: at release the fingers stood tangentially to the hole's motion, and a ball sinking into the moving hole was carried into an open fingertip and lifted back onto the platform (stuck). The release also had a systematic ~45 ms lag and a few-mm radial placement error.
rounds.how_found: A11/A14: the space around the target was never checked against the gripper, only the arm path against the planner; v2 had already shown that the planner does not model the gripper body. Ground-truth logs of failed episodes then showed the ball still touching a finger (held=True) when it stuck, after a clean landing over the hole.
rounds.why_missed: In the base scene the ball is alone and the default finger axis happened to be radial at the release point, so neither the grasp footprint nor the finger orientation at release ever mattered.
rounds.fix: Rank grasp candidates by the xy clearance of both open fingertips (centre +- 6 cm along the closing axis) to perceived obstacle footprints; before release turn the gripper about the vertical so the closing axis is radial (fingers out of the hole's tangential path); release higher (ball bottom 5.5 cm above the platform, fingertips clear of a ball sitting in the hole) with LEAD = 0.465 s + free-fall time computed from the height; correct the release position up to 3 times to within 2 mm.
rounds.general_rule: Check the gripper's own footprint (open fingertips, not just the planned arm) against neighbouring objects when choosing a grasp, and at release orient and retract the fingers so they are outside the region the released object will move through.

rounds.weakness: Two boxes beside the ball (on its +x and -y sides) blocked all four precomputed top-down grasp yaws, so the open fingers landed on a box every time (s_break 0.1). Generating extra yaws (every 15 deg, ranked by fingertip clearance) fixed the grasp at once in the probe, but the full check never reached 0.8 on every scene: the last four --all runs gave min 0.6-0.7, with base 0.9-1.0 and each variation fluctuating between 0.5 and 0.9 from run to run with identical code. Almost all remaining failures were 'ball stuck on platform': the timed drop through a hole only 5 mm wider than the ball.
rounds.how_found: Same assumption family as v4 (labelled parameter_tuning): v4's fix only chose among the four candidates the generator returned, so I asked what happens when none of them is clear.
rounds.why_missed: Not a design miss for the grasp (the fix was one function). The repair failed on a different, underlying weakness that v4 had already exposed: the drop's end-to-end error (release delay jitter ~+-20 ms = +-4 mm at the hole's 0.2 m/s, plus a 3-6 mm sideways push from the opening fingers whose direction depends on the gripper yaw) is about the size of the 5 mm clearance, so success per episode is ~0.75-0.85 and a 10-seed estimate swings +-0.15. I ran 4 of the 6 allowed repair iterations through the full check (extra yaws; a higher release with free-fall-derived timing plus never opening when the release pose was not reached; aiming 4-6 mm inside the orbit; landing 10 mm upstream of the hole) and tried a lighter grip before release in the probe only (it released the ball early), then stopped because no lever moved the release error below the clearance; per-seed ground truth showed the ball still sometimes resting on the rim with a centre error of only 4-6 mm.
rounds.fix: None kept: v5 marked unsolved and reverted; pipeline.py is the round-4 version (the v5 attempt is saved as dev/pipeline_v5_attempt.py).
rounds.general_rule: When success hinges on a tolerance near the noise floor, measure the full distribution of the actuation error (timing jitter and the displacement the actuator itself adds) on repeated trials before tuning means, and change the strategy (more margin, a closed-loop correction, or a second chance) when the tolerance is under about three standard deviations, because no single calibrated constant will make it reliable.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline never queried obstacles: plans only avoided the basket sweep and the apples, so two 24 cm posts beside the front approach were invisible. On the left side the open gripper clipped a post on the way to the pre-grasp (the arm then jammed against it) and the head-on straight-in move was geometrically blocked; only right-side seeds whose default heading already came from outside succeeded (s_break 0.3).
rounds.how_found: Assumption D1/D2 (nothing but the target, its neighbour and the basket occupies the workspace; get_obstacles() is never called) - the most common thing a real cluttered work cell violates.
rounds.why_missed: The base scene has no clutter, so every plan succeeded with an empty planner world; the pipeline was tuned to timing, grasp and drop, and obstacle handling was never exercised.
rounds.fix: Tried in 6 repairs (none reached 0.8 on v1; base 0.8-1.0, 1.0 at the end): pass get_obstacles() boxes (averaged over several noisy looks, padded 2 cm near the fruit and 6 cm in transit) to every plan; check the gripper's own swept volume (the planner models only the arm, not the ~16 x 13 cm open gripper) along pre-grasp -> pinch for 6 headings x 3 standoffs and try only clear candidates. Remaining failures: few clear headings for the left arm (2-3 cm clearance, so noise flips them), pre-grasps reached 3-5 cm off target after detours, and the search costs seconds inside a ~3 s ripeness window. Marked unsolved; the obstacle-aware code is kept (base 1.0).
rounds.general_rule: Before planning near a target, get the obstacles in the workspace, give them to the planner, and separately check the end effector's own swept volume against them, because motion planners often model only the arm links and a clipped tool jams the arm.

rounds.weakness: With an overhead rail running just above the fruit between the tree and the place zone, the pipeline failed on every seed: re-orienting the hand from its start pose (just in front of and above the rail) swept the open fingers onto the rail and jammed the arm, and after the pick the fixed 10 cm lift and the carry at that height would drive the gripper and fruit into the rail. The planner only keeps the arm links clear of the rail, not the hand or the held fruit.
rounds.how_found: Assumption A4/D3 (free space above the work zone: lift 10 cm after the pick and carry at that height), next after the approach corridor (round 1); overhead clutter (shelves, rails, cables) is common in real cells.
rounds.why_missed: Free space above the target was implicit: every motion after the pick was a fixed 'up, then over' recipe, and the first obstacle fix only checked the hand along the final approach, not during re-orientation, lift or carry.
rounds.fix: Tried in 6 repairs (v4 stayed at 0.0-0.1; base stayed 1.0): gripper swept-volume checks for every straight leg (lift only as high as clear, carry at the highest clear level, staging poses behind the pre-grasp entered from above or by descending first and turning the hand low in front of the rail), arm plans with and without obstacle boxes, unpadded boxes so start states are not 'in collision', and watching the basket until its turn on this side is seen. Remaining failures: the planner's long detours between waypoints (arm swinging up to 1.5 m or across the table), detours eating the ~3 s ripeness window, and the hand still clipping the rail while re-orienting. Marked unsolved; the swept-volume checks are kept (base 1.0).
rounds.general_rule: When the planner cannot model the tool or the held object, plan near clutter as short straight legs whose tool volume you check, re-orient the tool only where it has free space all around, and budget the time this takes against any deadline before committing to a detour.

rounds.weakness: A light 18 cm box standing right in front of each fruit closed every approach corridor; the pipeline only knew how to plan around obstacles, found no clear approach and gave up (0/10).
rounds.how_found: Assumption D2 (the straight-in segment to the target is free) attacked with a movable object instead of a fixed one, after rounds 1-2 showed that planning around clutter is hard here.
rounds.why_missed: The pipeline treated everything it did not want to touch as an immovable obstacle; it had no action that changes the scene to make room.
rounds.fix: If no approach is clear and removing a single object would open one, push that object aside first with the open hand: come down beside its far face near its top (straight vertical path checked for the hand), sweep it sideways out of the corridor, lift away, look again; if the arm cannot get beside the inner face, push from the outside towards the centre line. Also: estimate the ripe moment early and refine it only with samples taken before it (a straight-line fit through the colour peak breaks). Reached 0.5 (base 1.0) in 6 repairs; failures: one arm often cannot reach the inner face with a level hand (the planner reports success but the hand stops 3-5 cm off), using the idle arm instead was worse (0.0), and the extra 3-6 s of pushing pushes the pick past the ripeness window on some seeds.
rounds.general_rule: When light clutter blocks every way to the target, consider moving it out of the way (push it aside from a reachable side, then look again) instead of only planning around it, and budget that time against the task's deadline.

rounds.weakness: The belt-speed measurement from the head camera segmented the belt with absolute gray thresholds (belt darker than 110, motion above 12). Under dimmer, warmer light (35%) the table fell below the dark threshold, the belt top was never found, and the pipeline silently fell back to a nominal speed; the release timing was then off by up to 20% of a 6 s ride and half the blocks missed the moving bowl.
rounds.how_found: Listing what the camera code assumes about appearance: every threshold was a raw pixel value tuned on the default render, and lighting is the most common thing that differs between a lab and a deployment.
rounds.why_missed: The thresholds were chosen by looking at frames from one lighting condition, and the fallback (nominal speed) hid the perception failure instead of surfacing it; with the nominal speed the task still succeeded often enough to look plausible.
rounds.fix: Normalise each frame set by its own bright background (90th-percentile gray mapped to a fixed level) before applying the dark/motion/red thresholds; verified offline on frames at 0.2x, 0.35x and 1.8x light that the speed error stays within 1%.
rounds.general_rule: Make every image threshold relative to a reference measured in the same image (e.g. normalise by the background brightness), and treat a perception step that returns nothing as a failure to report or retry rather than silently substituting a nominal value.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline never asked for obstacles other than the belt and blocker, and planned every move with the planner's default world (table only). Two static bars over the belt ends (one beside the pick area) made the open fingers catch on a bar during the approach (the gripper then 'held' the bar), and the carried block was swept into a bar. Repairs that queried get_obstacles and cleared the bars by height exposed a second weakness: with the payload carried higher, long or fallback (orientation-free) plans let the arm pick a different joint configuration and swing; once a swing passed the held block low over the belt past the place line, the task's first-contact check failed for the episode.
rounds.how_found: Reading which motions pass obstacles to the planner: only the carry did, with a hand-picked list, while the planner models neither the open fingers nor the held object.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene nothing stands near the paths, so every planned move happened to be clear; a planner that returns success was treated as proof that the motion was harmless.
rounds.fix: Not recovered within the repair budget (best 0.7 with: obstacles from get_obstacles; transit and carry heights computed so fingertips and payload clear every box in the straight corridor; obstacle-aware orientation-holding plans first, table-only plans only for vertical moves, no free plans while holding; arrival checked after every move; grasp verified by lifting and re-detecting; pick-carry retried on loss). Remaining failures: the right arm's plans at the higher carry height wandered or failed (start inside inflated boxes, joint-configuration flips). Pipeline reverted to the round-1 version; the attempt is in dev/pipeline_v3_attempt.py.
rounds.general_rule: Give the motion planner every perceived obstacle on every move and separately clear whatever the planner does not model (open fingers, the held object) by explicit margins; then check after each move that the tool arrived and the payload is still held, and never accept an unconstrained replan while carrying something near a region where contact has consequences.

rounds.weakness: Two things broke under bars hung across the belt over the release zone. (1) The release point was one fixed spot (3.5 cm before the place line) and the gripper descended vertically onto it without checking what was above; the arm or the carried block hit the bar. (2) The camera belt-speed estimate measured the belt length as the longest dark run per image row; the bright bars split the run, so pixels-per-metre and the speed came out 10-60% wrong, and the release timing missed the moving bowl. Static occluders next to the matching window also biased the measured pattern shift towards zero (2-5%).
rounds.how_found: Questioning 'the release point is free': the pipeline used the edge of the allowed zone nearest the target because it shortens the ride, but never looked at that spot; a bracket or sensor over a conveyor's infeed is common.
rounds.why_missed: In the default scene the whole allowed zone was empty, so the first choice always worked; and the vision step was only tested on scenes where nothing lay across the belt.
rounds.fix: Release point: scan the allowed zone from the place line back towards the load edge and take the first spot whose vertical column (open-gripper footprint, from the belt up 35 cm) is free of every perceived obstacle; pass all perceived obstacles to the planner for the carry. Vision: join dark runs separated by short gaps before taking the belt's extent, and keep only pixels whose whole shift window is moving. Verified offline on all stored frame sets (default, lighting, camera, bars): speed error within 1%.
rounds.general_rule: When the goal allows a region rather than a point, choose the point inside it by checking that the tool's whole approach volume is free, and make image measurements of a surface robust to static things lying across it (bridge gaps, exclude stationary pixels from motion matching) instead of assuming an unobstructed view.

rounds.weakness: A guard cover over the middle 22 cm of the conveyor hid part of the belt from the head camera. The speed measurement took the belt's image length from one contiguous dark run per row (gaps up to 25 px joined); the cover cut the run into two pieces, so the length, the pixel scale and the speed were off by 2-4x (estimates of 0.17-0.22 m/s for a 0.06 m/s belt, or no estimate), and the release timing against the moving bowl became a coin flip.
rounds.how_found: Questioning C3 (both belt ends visible): after the bar fix the scale still depended on seeing one unbroken belt surface between two edges; guards and covers over conveyors are normal. v9 (14 cm cover) was rejected at 0.6 because a wrong timing still hits the bowl about half the time, so the cover was widened (v10).
rounds.why_missed: The round-3 fix only bridged narrow gaps; it still assumed the belt is one object in each row, rather than asking which pixels carry the moving pattern.
rounds.fix: Per row and frame, the belt extent is now the span of all dark pieces that carry the moving pattern (pieces without motion, such as an arm or a cover, do not count), then RANSAC over rows and median over frames as before. A second, independent scale (place line to load edge, oriented by the pattern's motion direction) is kept as a fallback when no full extent is found. Offline on every stored frame set (default, light, camera, bars, cover) the speed error is within 1%; eval: base, v1, v5, v10 all 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Make image measurements of a surface robust to static things lying across it (bridge gaps, exclude stationary pixels from motion matching) instead of assuming an unobstructed view.

rounds.weakness: Under a strongly red-tinted light (colour [1.0, 0.35, 0.3]) every gray belt pixel passed the 'red' test (R minus max(G, B) > 60 after brightness normalisation), so the whole belt was dropped from the pattern matching, no speed estimate came out, and the pipeline fell back to the nominal belt speed: release timing became a coin flip (s_break 0.5).
rounds.how_found: After round 1 normalised brightness, the remaining appearance assumption in the camera code was the colour test for the red place line and blocker, which silently assumes white light.
rounds.why_missed: Round 1 fixed the threshold for the symptom it saw (overall brightness) with one global gain instead of asking which reference every image test depends on; colour tests were left on raw channel differences.
rounds.fix: Normalise each colour channel separately by its own 90th percentile (white balance against the background) before any gray or colour test. Offline on all stored frame sets the speed error stays within 1%; eval: base 1.0, v1 0.9, v5 0.9 (the two misses were CUDA out-of-memory at reset, the pipeline never ran), v10 1.0, v11 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Make every image threshold relative to a reference measured in the same image (e.g. normalise by the background brightness), and treat a perception step that returns nothing as a failure to report or retry rather than silently substituting a nominal value.

tasks.goal: pick up the box drink from the basket

rounds.weakness: The program looked for a placement spot only in a fixed preferred area of the table. When movable clutter filled that area it fell back to the least-bad spot, or to spots under an overhanging cabinet. It moved the held 22 cm box along free planner paths, which ignore the held object, so the box was swept through the clutter and knocked out of the grasp or tilted. When a descent stopped short, it opened the gripper anyway and dropped the box from the air.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9 (free table space in a fixed region): real countertops are cluttered. Screening the frozen pipeline against a table filled with eight movable boxes gave 0.2 on 5 seeds; the gate measured 0.0 on 10.
rounds.why_missed: In the base scene the preferred area was always empty, so the spot fallback, the carry path of the held object and the release-height check were never exercised.
rounds.fix: Three repairs. (1) Search spots over the whole table: clearance from every detected obstacle footprint, using world-frame extents, and nothing hanging over the spot below the object's height plus 35 cm. (2) Release only after the descent reaches resting height; otherwise back up and try the next spot. (3) Transport the held object in straight segments: leave the container towards the robot at rim height, change height in place to a band 3 cm above everything under the path and below anything over it, cross, then descend vertically.
rounds.general_rule: Treat a held object as part of the robot: route it yourself through space you have checked for its full volume (the motion planner does not see it), pick destinations by measured clearance over the whole reachable surface instead of a preferred area, and only release it once it is at its resting height.

rounds.weakness: The program assumed the box stood upright. Its grasp points sat at fixed heights above an 'upright' bottom, its fingers closed horizontally whatever the box's axis, the lift height came from the upright half-height, and the box was put down in whatever orientation it had been grasped in. A box leaning about 34 deg against the basket wall was therefore grasped off its axis or carried tilted, and it toppled when released. Its orientation estimates came from one noisy detection.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the box stands upright): items in a basket often lean against the wall. Screening showed that a box pushed towards the far side settles leaning on every seed, and the frozen pipeline scored 0.0 on 5 seeds; the gate measured 0.1 on 10.
rounds.why_missed: In the base scene the box always stood upright, so nothing depended on its orientation, and taking the orientation from a single noisy detection never mattered.
rounds.fix: Average orientation as well as position over repeated detections. Put grasp points on the box's actual long axis, with the fingers closing perpendicular to it. Compute the lift from the box's lowest point (its vertical extent), not from an upright half-height. Once the box is carried over the free spot, turn it upright in the hand by rotating the gripper about the grasp point (5 cm higher if out of reach), then lower and release.
rounds.general_rule: Measure an object's actual orientation (averaging repeated detections) instead of assuming its canonical pose; grasp relative to its real axes; and before placing it, correct its orientation in the hand, in free space the arm can reach, to the pose the goal requires.

rounds.weakness: The program left the basket straight towards the robot and relied on shallow approaches from the robot's side, the only grasps from which the arm can lift the box 13 cm over the rim. A fixed 36 cm item standing in front of the basket blocks both: the exit sweeps the held box into it, and the hand passes over it too low on a shallow approach.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A8 (the path from the container towards the robot is free): counters hold kettles and paper-towel holders in front of baskets. The frozen pipeline scored 0.0 on 5 screening seeds and 0.2 at the gate; the expert scored 0.0.
rounds.why_missed: In every earlier scene the space between the robot and the basket was empty, so the exit direction and the approach side were never choices.
rounds.fix: Six repairs, none reached 0.8 on v3 while keeping v2. (1) Exit in the first direction whose swept path is clear: v3 0.1. (2) Add an approach from the workspace-centre side, open the gripper only when needed, lift fallbacks (move towards the robot, then pitch the hand shallower), checked by detection: v3 0.7. (3) Hold checks, upright low over the spot first, retry from the current state: v3 0.6, v2 0.8. (4) Shallow elevations first across all grasp heights: 0.5. (5) A lower grasp height: 0.3. (6) Retry with the other arm: 0.5, v2 0.7. Unsolved: where the basket sits on the microwave the box has to rise above the arm's comfortable reach, the item removes the approaches that still reach that high, and the fallbacks produce motions at the reach limit (tracking errors, cabinet and table contacts, tilted boxes). The pipeline was reverted to round 2.
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a grasp, check that the whole sequence it implies (grasp, lift high enough, exit along a clear path) stays inside the arm's comfortable reach; when obstacles remove those approaches, change the plan (another arm, another exit, first clearing the way) instead of stacking fallbacks that run the arm at its reach limit.

rounds.weakness: The program chose the destination once, before carrying the object, and lowered it there without looking again. A tray that slid onto that part of the counter during the carry was hit, so the box was set down on or against it and toppled.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A12 (nothing moves on its own): on a shared counter, other objects get pushed around while the robot works. Screening showed 0.4 on 5 seeds; the gate measured 0.4 on 10.
rounds.why_missed: Nothing in the earlier scenes moved, so an observation made before the carry was still true at the release.
rounds.fix: Right before lowering: wait until the scene is still (obstacle positions averaged over 4 detections, compared 0.5 s apart, up to 4 s); re-check the chosen spot's clearance against the current obstacles; if it is taken, choose a new free spot from the current state and carry there (up to 3 times).
rounds.general_rule: Re-observe the target area, and let moving things come to rest, immediately before an irreversible action such as a release: plans made earlier can be invalidated by the time they are executed.

rounds.weakness: The program judged its motions by the commanded positions. Under a 1.2 kg load the arm sagged 1-2 cm below the commanded height, so the lift check (TCP moved less than commanded) declared the lift incomplete and gave up, though the box had in fact cleared the rim; carry and release heights were off by the same sag.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5/A11 (a light box; the arm reaches the commanded heights while carrying it): full cartons weigh about 1 kg. Screening a 1.2 kg carton gave 0.2 on 5 seeds; the gate measured 0.2 on 10. The trace showed the lift reporting success and the pipeline stopping right after it.
rounds.why_missed: With a 0.1 kg box the commanded and the actual heights agreed, so checking the command looked like checking the world.
rounds.fix: Closed-loop heights from detection. Lift until the measured lowest point of the box clears the rim, correcting up to 4 times; corrections are capped at 4 cm beyond the first estimate, so a box sliding in the fingers is not chased upwards (an uncapped loop asked for a height outside the workspace). Before crossing, measure the box and top up any sag. Before releasing, measure the remaining gap to the table and lower by it. Two repairs; eval --all: base 0.8, v1 1.0, v2 0.9, v4 0.8, v5 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Judge every motion by its measured effect on the object, re-detecting after the move, not by what was commanded: loads, slip and tracking errors separate commanded from actual poses. Bound every corrective loop so it cannot chase a slipping object.

tasks.goal: Place the cup onto the coaster on the table

rejected.reason: invalid scene (seed 1): box_l moved 0.091 m while settling (interpenetration or unsupported)

rounds.weakness: The only grasp was a tilted pinch around the cup's upper body, sized for a 5 cm cup. On a cup 7-8 cm wide the 9 cm gripper had almost no clearance: the approach knocked the cup over, or the angled pads wedged it out of the hand on the lift. The fallback (the cup's annotated rim points) only had near-vertical approaches, which were unreachable for cups far from the robot.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5 (the cup is small and cup-shaped), because real cups and mugs vary in size; screening showed that a mug-sized cup (1.5x) drops the pipeline from 1.0 to 0.0, while clutter around the coaster, a moving coaster and a heavy cup did not break it.
rounds.why_missed: Phase 1 only saw the task's own cup models, all 4.9-5.5 cm wide, so the grasp was tuned to them and the object's size was never compared with the gripper's opening.
rounds.fix: Measure the cup's width and choose the grasp from it: a body grasp only if width + 2.5 cm fits the 9 cm opening, otherwise a rim pinch. The rim pinch tries the annotated rim points, then a tilted pinch of the wall facing the hand (55-85 deg, several azimuths, opening 0.5 so the inner finger clears the far wall). The back-out direction after release is read from the hand pose, so it works for either grasp.
rounds.general_rule: Choose the grasp from the object's measured size relative to the gripper opening (with clearance for perception noise), and keep a second grasp family that stays reachable when the first one is not.

rounds.weakness: When light objects stood 1.5 cm from the cup on every side, every approach was refused, and the pipeline kept searching more approach angles, arms and grasp types until the 120 s budget ran out. It never moved anything out of the way. Each grasp candidate also re-opened an already open gripper (~1 s), so the search alone used most of the time.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A2 (some approach to the cup is always free), because real tables are cluttered around cups. Screening: four movable boxes packed around the cup gave 0.0; fixed walls around the cup also gave 0.0, but probably leave no room for the gripper at all, so they were not gated.
rounds.why_missed: In Phase 1 the cup always stood on open table, and a refused motion was only ever answered with a different approach angle, never with a change to the scene.
rounds.fix: Find small movable objects within 7 cm of the cup (from get_obstacles, size-filtered so furniture is never moved). Clear the ones on the hand's side first, up to 3: a top-down grasp closing across the axis perpendicular to the cup, then set it down at a free reachable spot away from the cup, the coaster and the path between them. If one cannot be grasped, try the next. On the short final approaches, brushing the remaining light neighbours is allowed (their gaps are inside the planner's margin). Gripper motions that would change nothing are skipped.
rounds.general_rule: If the target is boxed in by small movable objects, move them to a free spot before grasping instead of searching more and more approach angles until the time runs out.

rounds.weakness: Each grasp was planned from one estimate of the cup taken before the arm moved, and every fallback candidate reused that estimate. A cup that slid 9 cm while the arm approached made every attempt close on empty space or knock the cup, until the time ran out. Nothing checked that the cup was still where the grasp had been planned.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A4 (the cup stays where it was estimated during the approach), because people and other actions move objects. Screening needed care: a plain push tipped the cup in this simulator (high default friction), so the push was combined with a slick cup and table, which let the cup slide 9 cm upright. A no-push control on the same slick surfaces scored 0.8, so the motion, not the slickness, broke the pipeline (0.0).
rounds.why_missed: In Phase 1 and the earlier rounds the cup never moved by itself, so one estimate per grasp sequence was always valid.
rounds.fix: Before clearing or grasping, wait until two averaged estimates 0.5 s apart agree within 1.5 cm (the cup is still). Right after reaching each pre-grasp pose, estimate again; if the cup moved more than 1.5 cm, abort, wait until it is still and replan from its new position. To keep the earlier crowded-cup variation within the time budget with these extra checks, objects are cleared with whichever arm reaches them, one at a time between grasp attempts, and set down with a quick lift-shift-lower instead of a full placement search.
rounds.general_rule: Re-measure the target right before the irreversible part of an approach and replan if it has moved; never reuse one estimate for a whole sequence of attempts.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed the cup stands upright. A cup lying on its side was carried to the coaster and set down lying, so its base centre (what the check measures) ended 3-4 cm off; nothing noticed that the object first had to be turned upright.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5 again from the orientation side, because cups get knocked over; screening gave 0.0 for a cup lying on its side, while an object lying on the coaster, a coaster at the back of the table and a divider between cup and coaster did not break the pipeline.
rounds.why_missed: Every earlier scene had the cup standing, so 'grasp' and 'place' were written for one orientation, with no step that checks or changes the object's orientation.
rounds.fix: Not recovered within 6 repairs (best 0.7; the round-3 pipeline is kept). Tried: (1) plan the final upright tilted grasp and map it back through the stand-up rotation -- no reachable candidate, because with the rim pointing away from the robot every downward final approach maps to an approach from the far side; (2) flip: top-down grasp across the lying cup, lift, quarter turn about the closing axis in whichever direction keeps the hand reachable (the cup may end on its base or rim), set down, regrasp -- worked in isolation, 0.5 in the full run; (3-5) tilted and shifted flip grasps, a cap on refused approaches, flipping only clearly lying cups, a higher grasp -- 0.3, 0.4, 0.7; (6) carry the stood-up cup straight to the coaster -- 0.4. The remaining failures were cups at the back or edge of the table where no flip grasp is reachable, episodes that ran out of the 120 s budget (stand-up plus pick-and-place is roughly twice the motion), and occasional cups flung by the physics during the turn. A flip test also showed that box extents cannot tell a squat cup's axis from a diameter; the axis has to come from the detected frame.
rounds.general_rule: Check an object's orientation before manipulating it, and if it must be turned, choose the turn direction and the grasp from reachability and budget the extra motions (re-orienting costs about as much as the whole pick-and-place) before committing.

rounds.weakness: Clutter was only cleared around the object to pick, never around the place to put it down. With light objects packed around the coaster, the cup could not be lowered between them, or tipped against them, and the pipeline ran out of time. Two more weaknesses showed while repairing: a fully opened gripper swung its fingers into neighbours at release and knocked the cup; and a 'not quite centred' check on noisy estimates restarted a pick-and-place that could not finish in the remaining time, so placements already inside the success tolerance ended with the cup in a closed hand.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (nothing next to the coaster) after round 2 had covered the pick side; screening gave 0.2. The first design (v5) was rejected by the validity gate: on one seed of ten, a box started inside the furniture.
rounds.why_missed: The clearing added in round 2 was written for the pick only; the placement path and the end-of-task correction were never tested with neighbours close by or with little time left.
rounds.fix: Before picking (both hands free), clear up to 2 light objects crowding the coaster, with the round-2 routine generalised to any target; brush the rest on the final descent. Grasp boxes 4.5 cm below their top and check they are still held after the lift (a 2.5 cm pinch slipped and the same box was 'cleared' twice). Release with the gripper opened only to the cup's width + 1.5 cm. Re-place only if a 16-sample estimate is off by more than 1.2 cm AND at least 45 s of the 120 s remain. Grasp the cup body lower (0.15 of its height above centre) so a slick cup swings less. Six repairs were needed; each full check varied by about 0.2 per scene between runs.
rounds.general_rule: Clear the spot where an object will be put down as well as where it is picked up, before picking it up while the hands are free; and never start a corrective retry that cannot finish in the remaining time, because a near miss with an open hand beats a timed-out retry holding the object.

rounds.weakness: Each grasp and lift assumed free space above the cup: lifting was always straight up, and refused approaches were retried without limit. With the cup at the back of the table next to a low bookcase, the straight lift was refused, the 'held' cup was lost, and eight near-identical refused re-approaches (~6 s each) used up the time.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A10 (one arm comfortably reaches both objects) with the cup at the back on one side and the coaster at the front edge on the other; screening gave 0.4 and the gate 0.5.
rounds.why_missed: Earlier scenes never put the cup next to furniture, so lifting straight up and retrying approaches were always cheap.
rounds.fix: Not recovered (one repair, 0.3); the round-5 pipeline is kept. The repair backed away along the approach when the straight lift was refused, and gave up an arm after 4 refused final approaches. It stopped there because the variation is flawed: the furniture layout changes with the seed, and in 5 of 10 seeds the fixed cup position (0.10, 0.12) lies inside the low bookcase's footprint (4-5 cm overlap in x and y), i.e. in its lower compartment under a fixed overhang. The validity check did not catch this, since nothing interpenetrates. Those 5 seeds are a different task that the padded planner cannot approach, so 0.8 was unreachable whatever the pipeline did; the other failures were cups tipping at a coaster very close to the robot.
rounds.general_rule: When placing objects at fixed coordinates in scenes whose furniture moves between instances, check every instance for containment under furniture, not just collisions; and retry a refused approach only a few times, then change strategy instead of repeating it until the time runs out.

rounds.weakness: The cup's width was taken from the world-axis extent of its detected box. For a cup turned about 45 deg this overestimates the diameter by up to 41% (0.12 m for a 7.3-8.3 cm mug). So the grasp choice and the clutter gaps were computed from a cup that seemed much wider than it was. Mild in open scenes (some normal cups were sent rim-first), but with a mug-size cup boxed in by light objects, nothing fitted and the time ran out.
rounds.how_found: After nine single-axis screenings in this round failed to break the pipeline, combined two axes that had each broken and recovered (a mug-size cup and packed clutter); screening gave 0.3. A profile of one failure printed the cup width the pipeline used, which was far larger than the cup.
rounds.why_missed: The width helper was written in round 1 and only ever checked on cups that happened to be nearly axis-aligned; its result was never compared with the object's known size.
rounds.fix: Measure the width in the object's own frame: the larger of the two box extents that are not the vertical axis. One repair: base 0.9, v1 0.9, v2 0.8, v3 0.8, v6 0.9, v8 0.8.
rounds.general_rule: Measure an object's size in its own frame, not from its world-axis bounding box, before using it to choose a grasp or a clearance, and sanity-check derived sizes against what the object can plausibly be.

tasks.goal: put the spoon on the plate

rounds.weakness: The program detected the plate once, before picking up the spoon, and released the spoon at that position; the plate had been slid 7 cm while the spoon was being picked, so every spoon landed 7 cm off the plate centre.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1: the goal location was perceived once at the start of a multi-second manipulation; on a real robot a person or another process can move the target while the arm is busy.
rounds.why_missed: The first version treated the goal pose as fixed scene knowledge read once, because nothing moved in the nominal scenes.
rounds.fix: Detect the plate after the pick, tracking it over short windows until it is stationary; check it again right before releasing and carry the spoon over its new position if it moved more than 1.5 cm.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive the goal location right before acting on it and after every long step, waiting until it is stationary, instead of reusing an estimate taken before the manipulation began.

rounds.weakness: The program took every grasp from the object's annotated grasp frames. With the spoon lying upside down those frames pointed into the counter, every candidate's pre-grasp pose was below the counter top, and the program gave up without trying any other grasp.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A4: the grasp library assumes the object rests in its nominal orientation, and on a real counter utensils and tools are often flipped or turned on their side.
rounds.why_missed: In every nominal scene the object rested the right way up, so the library grasp always produced a reachable candidate and I never checked what it depended on.
rounds.fix: When the library grasp finds no candidate, derive a top-down grasp from the current bounding box: vertical approach onto the object's frame point, fingers closing across its longest horizontal axis, fingertips just above its underside.
rounds.general_rule: Do not depend on one grasp source tied to an object's nominal pose; when it yields nothing, derive a grasp from the object's currently observed geometry, approaching vertically and closing across its narrow horizontal dimension just above its underside.

rounds.weakness: The program trusted a single top-down pinch of a heavier, slippery spoon: the grip held for the first 1-2 cm of the lift, then the spoon slid down out of the fingers. The program repeated near-identical grasps, and its own fallback grasp descended so close to the counter that the planner refused the last centimetres.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5: a top-down pinch of a flat object holds it by friction alone, and real utensils are wet, greasy or heavier than the nominal one.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal spoon weighs 50 g, so any pinch held it, and I never checked a grasp before carrying the object.
rounds.fix: Lift 3 cm and check the hold before the full lift; on a slip, release, detect again and re-grasp differently (at the box centre as a centre-of-mass guess, at another fingertip height, shifted along the object); let the short final descent of the fallback grasp touch the counter so that it is not refused. A wrist roll that put a finger under the object did not help and was removed.
rounds.general_rule: Check every grasp with a short test lift before carrying, and when the object slips, change the grasp (nearer the centre of mass, another contact height or position) instead of repeating the one that just failed.

rounds.weakness: With the spoon partly under a low overhang, every grasp the program tried was under or right next to the overhang: the library grasp and the grasp at the object's frame point were blocked, and their partial descents pushed the spoon further in. The exposed end (7.5 cm) is shorter than the hand needs (about 6 cm along the object plus the planner's safety margin), so even a grasp chosen there by a clearance check, vertical or tilted 20-35 degrees from the open side, was refused on its approach.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A4: the program assumed there is room for the hand above its grasp point; on real counters utensils lie partly under shelves, boards and other items.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scenes nothing is above the spoon, so I never checked the space the hand needs before reaching.
rounds.fix: Not recovered in 3 repairs (best 0.0): a clearance check over the hand's footprint along the object, checking that space before any reach, a tilted approach from the open side, and stopping when the object has been knocked off the counter. Moving the object into the open first (a push) would also need the hand next to the overhang. Variation reverted; the pipeline is back at round 3.
rounds.general_rule: Before reaching, check that the whole hand plus the planner's safety margin fits around the grasp point, because a reach that is refused halfway still pushes the object deeper into clutter; if no point on the object has that room, the object must be moved into the open before it can be grasped.

rounds.weakness: The same weakness as v8 with more of the spoon exposed (about 10 cm of the bowl end): the program's grasps are at or near the spoon's middle, under the overhang, and a refused reach still pushes the spoon. Choosing a grasp point on the exposed end by checking the space above it recovered 3 of 10 seeds; most approaches to that end were still refused or used up the episode budget.
rounds.how_found: Repeated v8's question (room for the hand above the grasp point) with an exposure long enough for the hand, to separate 'no room anywhere' from 'room, but not where the program grasps'.
rounds.why_missed: The program never asked where on the object there is room for the hand; its re-grasps only move 3 cm along the object.
rounds.fix: Not recovered in 2 repairs (best 0.3): grasp points along the object filtered by the hand's footprint against the obstacle boxes, checked before any reach (0.3); the footprint widened by the planner's margin (0.2, more episodes out of budget). The approach of the whole arm, not only the hand, has to clear the overhang. Variation reverted; the pipeline is back at round 3.
rounds.general_rule: Before reaching, check that the whole hand plus the planner's safety margin fits around the grasp point, because a reach that is refused halfway still pushes the object deeper into clutter; if no point on the object has that room, the object must be moved into the open before it can be grasped.
