rounds.weakness: The put-down (handover) spot was a hard-coded table coordinate. With a fixed block standing there, the left arm drove the mug into the block and knocked it off; the right arm then had nothing graspable (10/10 failures). The program had no notion of free space, of other supporting surfaces, or of whether the second arm could reach the object where the first arm leaves it. Repair exposed three more weaknesses: grasps tried only the first reachable candidate even when its final approach was blocked, the pre-place pose 5 cm above a raised surface was out of reach, and a placement that 'succeeded' could leave the mug where the other arm cannot grasp it.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the hard-coded handover spot is empty): it is the only location in the program that is a constant instead of something perceived, and real tables are cluttered.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the spot is always free and the expert's coordinates suit both arms, so the choice of spot never had to be justified or checked.
rounds.fix: Put-down spot chosen at run time: candidates are free table cells (>= 8 cm from averaged obstacle footprints, roomy ones first) and flat tops of perceived boxes wide enough for the mug body. A candidate is used only if the receiving arm has a reachable grasp of the mug at that hypothetical pose and the placing arm's placement plans (pre-approach shortened to 2 cm for raised surfaces). The planner gets inflated obstacle boxes; grasps fall through all reachable candidates; the landing is verified (upright, within 4 cm). Recovered to 0.6 only: the block occupies exactly the zone both arms reach, so feasible spots sit at the edge of both workspaces and depend on which grasp the first arm happened to take.
rounds.general_rule: Never hard-code where an object is put down or handed over; choose the spot at run time from perceived free support surfaces (including tops of objects) and accept it only if both the placing motion and the next arm's grasp there are reachable.

rounds.weakness: Arm roles were hard-coded: the left arm always fetched and the right arm always hung. With the rack on the far left the right arm could not reach the hook (0/10). Repair exposed three deeper faults in the hang itself. The carry to the hook was planned without the rack, so the mug in the hand swept into the rack's post and turned in the grip. The in-hand pose measured right after lifting was stale by the time the handle reached the hook (off by 3-12 cm and up to ~50 deg), so the single precomputed insertion missed and the mug fell. And a correction move that also held the gripper orientation was infeasible, because the corrected pose has a different orientation.
rounds.how_found: Three earlier designs (a 0.35 kg slippery mug, the rack turned 1 rad, the mug moved to the right half) were all rejected because the frozen pipeline still scored 0.8. The remaining hard-coded choice in the program was which arm does which job (A3), so I moved the goal fixture to the other side.
rounds.why_missed: In every nominal layout the rack stands on the right, so assigning arms by habit always worked. The hang was only ever executed by the arm whose carry path happens to stay clear of the rack, so the in-hand drift never mattered.
rounds.fix: Arm roles now come from the scene: the arm on the hook's side hangs, and the mug is handed over only if it starts on the other side. The mug is carried slowly to a staging pose 12 cm out along the hook axis, with the rack as an obstacle, then waits 0.5 s to settle. At the hook's mouth the measured handle is servoed onto the entrance (re-measure, correct, up to 3 times, ignoring implausible jumps over 8 cm). The handle then slides in slowly on a fixed gripper orientation, falling back to an unconstrained slide.
rounds.general_rule: Decide which arm does what from the perceived layout, not by habit, and before a precision insertion re-measure the held object at the target's entrance and correct until it is aligned, because objects shift and turn in the hand while they are carried.

rounds.weakness: The rack was measured once before the hang. Staging, servo and slide all aimed at that pose, so a rack pushed ~8 cm during the carry made every insertion miss (0/10). The round-2 servo loop corrected only the held mug, never the hook it aimed at. Repair exposed a second staleness: waiting for the target to come to rest while holding the mug made the in-hand pose measured before the wait wrong too (the mug settles in the hand during any pause). That put the staging pose out of reach and briefly dropped the base task to 0.7.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A6 for the target instead of the grasped object. The servo added in round 2 re-measures only what is in the hand. Two other designs failed to break the pipeline: clutter sliding into the handover spot was absorbed because the spot is chosen late.
rounds.why_missed: In every scene so far the rack was fixed, so perceiving the target once was always valid, and the round-2 repair treated the target pose as ground truth.
rounds.fix: Before the hang, wait until the rack is still: two 40-sample averages 1 s apart within 8 mm, for up to 10 s. Measure the in-hand mug only after that wait. In the servo loop, re-measure the hook every iteration and re-aim (waiting for stillness again) if it moved by more than 1 cm. Final eval: base 0.8, v5 0.9, v7 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Right before a precision step, re-measure the target as well as the held object, wait until the target is still, and take every measurement the step uses after the last pause, because both the target and the object in hand can move while you wait.

rounds.weakness: Everything about the hang was tuned to RoboTwin's mugs 0-9. With the larger, unseen mug 12, the grasp chosen by preference left the hook unreachable on most seeds (the handle sits further from the grip), and the program just pushed on. Repairs uncovered three more faults. The fixed insertion stalled: the big loop met the hook's tip and was held back while the gripper slid along it, so the handle stopped 7-10 cm short. The program then released anyway, because a completed motion was taken as a completed insertion. And after a good hang, the retreat move failed, an immediate check of the still-swinging mug said 'not hung', and the arm's return home knocked it off the rack.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9 (the mug is the size of the training mugs). RoboTwin ships three mug models the task never uses, and model 12 is the largest; a real robot meets mugs of every size.
rounds.why_missed: All training mugs are similar enough that the default grasp, the fixed 5 cm insertion and an open-loop release always worked, so neither grasp choice nor engagement was ever checked.
rounds.fix: Six repairs: (1) if a hang move is unreachable with the current grasp, put the mug back and regrasp with an untried contact point; (2) after release, withdraw along the approach axis as far as is reachable, then lift, and judge success only after the mug settles, never touching a hung mug again; (3) a stepwise slide with lateral gating (worse, reverted); (4) insertion depth computed from the rack's geometry, with a tighter servo; (5) release only if the handle is measured past the tip, otherwise keep holding, back out and regrasp; (6) when the insertion stalls, search +-1.5 cm offsets across the axis. v8 peaked at 0.3 (repairs 1 and 5) and ended at 0.2. The base task and the accepted v5 and v7 all reached 1.0 with these repairs. The expert, with ground truth, also fails v8 10/10, which suggests this model's handle keypoint does not describe an opening the hook can thread from this approach.
rounds.general_rule: Never take a finished motion as a finished insertion: before letting go, measure that the object is actually engaged at its goal, and if it is not, keep holding it, back out, and retry with a different alignment or grasp; after letting go, withdraw along a verified-free path and judge the result only once the object has settled.

rounds.weakness: The program assumed the object can always be grasped where it lies. Every grasp it uses comes from above, followed by a straight lift. With a shelf 2 cm above the mug no grasp was plannable, and the program gave up at once (0/10): it had no way to change where the object is before grasping it. Repairs showed that the motions needed to slide the mug out sit at the edge of the arms' reach. Low horizontal gripper poses are mostly unreachable, the wrist cannot pass under an inflated obstacle box, the arm that looks natural for a direction is often the one that cannot get in, and a push that only just clears the overhang leaves the object where the next grasp collides with it or out at the table edge.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7 (the space above the object is free): all the object's grasp points are approached from above and every grasp ends in a straight lift, so anything overhead removes every option at once.
rounds.why_missed: Nothing ever stood above an object in the nominal scenes, so the approach direction was never a choice and grasping 'where it lies' always worked.
rounds.fix: Detect overhangs: perceived boxes whose footprint covers the object and whose underside is above the table. Then slide the object out before grasping, with the closed gripper pointing forward and tilted 17 deg down (reachability probes showed horizontal poses at table height are mostly unreachable). Try every arm/direction pairing and three contact offsets toward the open edge, plan against the overhang's perceived box rather than an extra-inflated one, push 7 cm clear, prefer exits towards the table's middle, and verify the object is actually clear. Reached 0.2 (base, v5 and v7 stayed at 1.0).
rounds.general_rule: When an object cannot be grasped where it is, first move it to where it can be (for example slide it out with a push the arm can actually reach, trying each arm and direction), and confirm it is clear and reachable before planning the grasp.

rounds.weakness: After the hand-over, the program checked that the mug stood within 4 cm of where it was set down and gave up the whole task if not. A mug nudged ~10 cm right after release made every episode stop at that check (0/10), although the mug was still upright and perfectly graspable where it ended up.
rounds.how_found: Read the checks added in earlier rounds and asked what each does when it fails: the landing check was the only one whose failure branch aborted instead of re-planning.
rounds.why_missed: The check was written to catch a mug that fell over during placement. In every scene so far a mug that was not at the spot had also fallen over, so 'not where I put it' and 'unrecoverable' always coincided.
rounds.fix: After the hand-over, wait until the mug is still (two 40-sample averages 1 s apart), then continue from where it actually is if it is upright; whether it still sits on a raised support is decided from its measured height. Before every grasp of the hanging arm, also wait until the mug is still. Final eval: base 0.9, v5 1.0, v7 1.0, v13 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: When a check finds the world different from what the plan expected, treat it as new information: wait until things are still, re-perceive, and continue from the actual state, and abort only if the task has really become impossible.

rounds.weakness: Obstacles were measured once, at the start. A tall post that glided in after the first look, ending between the hand-over area and the rack, was invisible to every later plan: the mug in the hanging arm was swung into it, turned in the grip, and every pose computed from the garbled in-hand measurement was absurd (0/10). Repairs exposed further faults. The planner models only the arm, so carries planned around obstacles still drove the held mug into them. When the scene changed next to the mug, the hanging arm could no longer approach it, and the program had no way to move it again. The extra safety margin on obstacle boxes closed the real gap beside the mug. A failed put-back left the mug dangling while the other arm reached for it.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A13: the obstacle list is computed once at the start, and in round 6 only the mug was allowed to move. People and objects entering the workspace mid-task are the commonest change a real robot sees.
rounds.why_missed: In every scene so far, everything that was in the way was already there at the first look, so one obstacle snapshot per episode was enough.
rounds.fix: Six repairs: (1) re-perceive the obstacles (waiting until they are still) before each phase and plan with the fresh boxes; (2) while carrying, plan against obstacles grown by how far the held mug sticks out, lifting straight up before turning; (3) if the hanging arm can no longer take the mug, have the other arm move it to a spot chosen from the current scene; (4) plan grasps against the obstacles as perceived, without the extra margin; (5) reliable put-back and release before a regrasp or redo; (6) stage closer to the hook when the usual staging pose is blocked. v16 stayed at 0.0-0.1. The base task and the accepted v5, v7 and v13 stayed at 0.9-1.0 throughout.
rounds.general_rule: Re-perceive obstacles before every phase rather than once per task, plan carrying motions against obstacles enlarged by the held object's extent, and when a change in the scene blocks the next step, redo the previous step from the current scene instead of giving up.

rounds.weakness:
The program had no way to make room. With tall movable objects standing a finger's width from the mug on all four sides, every grasp approach was refused and the program gave up (0/10). Repairs exposed the parts of 'making room' it lacked:
- Crowding objects have no grasp keypoints, so they need a manual grasp from straight above.
- A pinch can miss, and the object must be re-detected before retrying.
- The nearest free spot is usually in the working corridor, so a moved object becomes the next obstacle.
- Far-out spots are often out of reach.
- Planning from among crowding objects fails outright, because the arm already sits inside their safety margins.
- An object released above the table falls over and becomes a new obstacle.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A12 (only the task objects are near the mug): real counters are crowded, and every grasp the program knows needs free space around the object.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal table holds only the mug and the rack, so some grasp approach was always free and 'make room first' never came up.
rounds.fix:
Six repairs:
(1) When no grasp works, find movable objects crowding the mug, move them one at a time with a straight-down grasp, re-perceive, and retry.
(2) Re-detect and turn the fingers 90 deg after a missed pinch; send objects far out on the arm's own side.
(3) Choose destinations about 0.36 m out, within reach.
(4) Return home before clearing, and lift clear of the crowd after the grasp.
(5) If every plan fails with the safety margins, retry against the boxes as perceived.
(6) Always set a moved object down before releasing it, and lift the held mug to a safe height.
v17 reached 0.2-0.3. The base task and the accepted v5, v7 and v13 ended at 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: When the target is boxed in, make room first: move the neighbours one at a time to reachable spots outside the working corridor, set each one down before letting go, and plan every next motion from a free start (lift clear of the crowd), re-perceiving after each move.

rounds.weakness: The hand-over assumed that some table spot is reachable by both arms. A fixed divider between the arms' halves left no such spot except awkwardly around the divider's front end. The program then tried spot after spot, each pre-place move succeeding and each final descent being refused, and gave up when its list ran out (8/10 failed). The in-air hand-over added in repair exposed a reach problem: the fetching arm holds the mug with its wrist ~23 cm above it, so lifting the mug over a 30 cm divider asks for gripper poses near 1.33 m, out of reach. Asking the placement helper for the mug's current orientation also re-aligned the mug and swung the gripper 20 cm sideways.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7 for the hand-over: after the hand-over spot became a run-time choice (round 1), the program still assumed open table connects the two arms' halves.
rounds.why_missed: The table was always open between the arms, so the spot search always found a common spot and no other hand-over mode was ever needed.
rounds.fix: Four repairs: (1) an in-air hand-over when no table spot works for both arms (hold the mug above the obstacle, the other arm grasps it, the first lets go); (2) carry the held mug by pure translation of the gripper; (3) hold it just above the obstacle's true top, lowest first; (4) extend the spot search toward the divider's end and try more spots. v20 stayed at 0.2. The run's time budget ended here, so the variation was stopped after 4 of the 6 allowed repairs. Base and the accepted variations stayed at 0.8-1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Before committing to a hand-over, check that a hand-over pose exists that both arms can actually reach (a shared surface, around an obstacle's end, or in the air at a reachable height), and choose the fetching arm's grasp so its wrist does not put that pose out of reach.

tasks.goal:
use one arm to open the cabinet's drawer, and the other arm to put the object on the table into
the drawer

rounds.weakness: The pipeline never looked at the space it needed. A movable 18 cm box standing in front of the bottom drawer made the planner refuse every approach to the handle (10/10 seeds: 'no collision-free path'), and nothing in the pipeline could remove it. Repair exposed two hidden weaknesses: the default grasp of a box-shaped obstacle only tried two top-down yaws, both unreachable near the robot's centre line; and the drawer pull was open-loop: on some seeds the gripper slipped off the handle while the hand finished all pull steps 'successfully', the drawer stayed shut, and the object was then dropped in front of the closed drawer.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5 (the space in front of the drawer is free). Real drawers have things parked in front of them, and the pipeline left obstacles entirely to the planner, which can route around an obstacle but never remove it; in front of a drawer there is no way around.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the table in front of the cabinet is empty, so a planner-only strategy and an unverified pull always worked; the slipped-handle case was masked because one noisy grasp in ten happened to hold.
rounds.fix: Before touching the handle, compute the volume the drawer and the pulling hand sweep (cabinet face to opening + 25 cm along the pull direction, +-20 cm sideways, table to handle + 15 cm); every non-task obstacle (boxes averaged over 5 get_obstacles calls) overlapping it is picked up (fallback grasp search over 12 top-down yaws and 8 side directions, opening sized to the box) and set down on a free table spot on that arm's side, then the volume is re-checked; an obstacle that cannot be moved is remembered. The pull is now closed-loop: after each 3.5 cm step the handle's travel is measured by detection, and if the grasp is lost or the handle stops following, it is re-grasped where it is (3 attempts); placing is skipped if the drawer is open < 10 cm. The drop orientation turns the finger closing axis along the drawer front so the fingers cannot touch the cabinet face above.
rounds.general_rule: Before any motion that needs free space, compute the whole volume the robot and the moved part will sweep and clear movable objects out of it (verifying they left), and close the loop on every contact motion by measuring the manipulated object's own displacement instead of trusting the robot's motion status.

rounds.weakness: Every step assumed open space above the work: the pull grasp opened the gripper fully (its upper finger reaches 12 cm above the handle), and the object was always lowered into the drawer from above with a top-down grip. With a fixed board overhanging the drawer 9 cm above the handle, the full-open handle grasp hit the board, the clearing step tried to pick up the board itself, and there was no way to put the object in from above.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A5/A9 (the space above the opened drawer is free). Real drawers often sit under a counter or shelf, and every motion in the pipeline came down from above.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene nothing is above the drawer, so the default full-open grip and top-down placement were never constrained.
rounds.fix: Not recovered in 5 of 6 repairs (best: drawer opened on 3/10 seeds, 0/10 success); variation marked unsolved and the pipeline reverted to round 1. Tried: treat boxes too wide to grip as immovable furniture; a low-profile handle grip (horizontal approach, fingers closing vertically, opening sized to the clearance under the board) searched over 9 approach directions and both wrist rolls; precise handle height from 30 averaged detections; a side grip of the object with the fingers pointing into the drawer and a horizontal insertion between the drawer's front wall and the board. Why it failed: the handle sits ~1.5 cm under the next drawer, so a vertical pinch has a few-mm window (too high and the fingers grip the drawer above), smaller than the remaining perception error; one arm cannot reach under the board at all; and each added step (side pick near the table, insertion through a 7 cm gap) failed often enough that the chain never completed.
rounds.general_rule: Before choosing a strategy, compute the clearance envelope each step actually needs (gripper opening, finger length, wrist and forearm) against the space around the target, and if a step's tolerance is smaller than your perception error, change the approach (a different grip, a different arm, or a different place) rather than repeating the same step more precisely.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed the drawer always reaches its full travel: it pulled a fixed 17 cm, gave up below 10 cm, and aimed the drop at a fixed 6 cm behind the handle. A fixed low block stopping the drawer after ~9 cm broke every step: the clearing step 'moved' the fixed block with an empty hand (the grip reported holding, the block never rose), the fully open fingers no longer fit between handle and block, the pull retried a hard stop three times, and the pipeline gave up.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3/A10 (the drawer opens to its full travel). Real drawers are often stopped short by clutter, a door or a short runner, and every number in the drop step was a nominal offset, not a measurement.
rounds.why_missed: The nominal drawer always opened fully, so fixed thresholds and offsets were never wrong.
rounds.fix: Repairs (2 of 6, best 0.2; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): verify that a grasped obstacle actually rises before carrying it (fixed things are recognised at once); fall back to a partly open handle grip when the full-open grasp has no free path; treat two stalls at the same opening while the handle is still held as a hard stop and continue with that opening; compute the drop point from the measured gap between the drawer's front wall and the cabinet face; drop slowly with contact monitoring when the planner's margin exceeds the real clearance. Why unsolved: with ~9 cm of travel the exposed gap (~7.5 cm) is barely wider than the hand (6.2 cm), and the 6-DoF arms reach the required top-down pose within ~1 cm of the cabinet face only on ~2/10 layouts, so the variation is close to infeasible for this robot (my design error: I did not check reachability before gating it).
rounds.general_rule: Treat every action's outcome as a measurement: when a step achieves less than planned (a part stops early, an object does not rise), re-derive the following targets from the measured state and check that they are still reachable with the gripper's real envelope before acting, instead of continuing with nominal offsets or retrying the same step.

rounds.weakness: The drawer's opening was measured as the handle's travel in the world from where it was first seen. When the light cabinet slid 12 cm towards the robot while the drawer was being reached for and pulled, the handle's travel counted as opening: the pull stopped with the drawer open only a few cm, and every drop pose was then unreachable (10/10 seeds).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A6 (the scene is static). Light furniture moves when a drawer is dragged, and the round-1 progress measurement used a world-fixed reference that assumes the cabinet stays put.
rounds.why_missed: The cabinet is fixed in the nominal scene, so the world frame and the cabinet frame coincide and the measurement looked correct; round 1 had just introduced it as the fix for an open-loop pull.
rounds.fix: The opening is now the handle's offset from the cabinet body along the pull direction (both re-detected and averaged at every check) minus its closed value, so the pull continues until the drawer is open relative to the cabinet, wherever the cabinet goes. One repair.
rounds.general_rule: Measure a manipulation's progress in the frame of the object being manipulated (relative to its own body or base, re-detected each time), never against a world reference recorded earlier, because the supporting object can move while you act on it.

rounds.weakness: The drawer was pulled at the planner's normal speed through a friction pinch on a thin handle bar. With stiff runners (damping 60 N s/m) the resisting force exceeded what the pinch could hold: the handle slipped out after a few cm each time, three re-grasps opened the drawer only 5-10 cm, and the drop then failed (2/10). Repair also exposed that reaching for the handle while the cabinet itself was still moving closed the gripper on the cabinet body instead.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A3/A8 (the drawer slides easily, so a pinch grip holds). Real drawers stick and drag; the pull speed was never chosen, only inherited from the planner.
rounds.why_missed: In the nominal scene the drawer needs almost no force, so speed and grip strength never mattered, and the closed-loop re-grasp from round 1 hid the slips as long as the drawer was free.
rounds.fix: Pull at slow speed in 3.5 cm steps (resistance from the runners grows with speed; smaller 1 cm steps were tried and failed because each step's progress drowned in detection noise), allow up to 6 re-grasps from wherever the handle is, and wait until the cabinet and the object are still (two averaged detections 0.5 s apart within 8 mm) before reaching for them. Two repairs; base 1.0, v1 1.0, v5 0.9, v6 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: When moving something against resistance, slow down (drag forces grow with speed and a friction grip holds only so much), size each step so its expected progress is well above your measurement noise, re-grasp from the current position whenever the grip slips, and never start a grasp while the target or its support is still moving.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed a small object: top-down grasp with the gripper pre-opened to width + 2 cm (capped at full opening), a drop 6-12 cm above an aim point 6 cm behind the handle. Scaled 1.5x, cubes and boxes no longer fit between the fingers (no collision-free grasp), and long objects dropped like that landed across the drawer's front wall or against the cabinet face.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A7 (the object is small). Real objects vary in size and the pipeline never compared the object's dimensions with the gripper's capacity or with the size of the opening it is dropped into.
rounds.why_missed: All nominal objects are 3-7 cm across, well within the gripper and the drawer gap.
rounds.fix: None: marked unsolved without repairs. Three of ten seeds are a rubik's cube that becomes 10 cm on every side, wider than the 9 cm maximum gripper gap; carrying it with both arms would need synchronized dual-arm motion, which the API does not offer. The variation therefore cannot reach 0.8 (my design error: I did not check the scaled sizes against the gripper before gating).
rounds.general_rule: Before planning a grasp or a placement, compare the object's measured dimensions with the gripper's maximum opening and with the free space at the destination, and choose the grasp axis, the orientation and the release height from that comparison, declaring the task infeasible for this gripper when no axis fits.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline assumed the object stands alone with room for the open fingers on some side; the clearing from round 1 only looked at the drawer's work volume. With the object packed between three blocks (1.6 cm gaps, fingers 3.7 cm thick) every grasp was refused and nothing made room (10/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A12/A5 at the grasp (the object stands alone). Items in trays and crowded shelves are packed against each other.
rounds.why_missed: Round 1 generalised clearing only to the volume the drawer and the pulling hand sweep, not to the volume the fingers need around the object.
rounds.fix: Repairs (4 of 6, best 0.3; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): when no grasp of the object has a free path, move neighbouring movable obstacles away (verifying they rose) and retry; grasp blocks at their free ends, not only at their centre; prefer blocks whose ends stick out past the object; pull the drawer slowly only after a first stall to save time. Found on the way: the stillness check from round 3 compared two 5-sample averages with an 8 mm tolerance, below the noise of their difference, so it waited on still objects for seconds. Why unsolved: freeing a grasp axis needs two block moves (~20-30 s each), and with the drawer sequence this exceeds the 120 s episode budget whenever anything is retried.
rounds.general_rule: Before acting on a target, reserve the volume your fingers (not just your arm) need around it and plan which neighbours to move as a whole within the time budget, and set every threshold for 'did it move' well above the noise of the measurement it is compared with.

rounds.weakness: Arms were assigned by a fixed rule (object to the arm on its side, drawer to the other). With the cabinet 20 cm to the right, the left arm could not reach the handle or the drop zone, and a right-side object stood in the drawer's path: the opening drawer knocked it off the table.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1/A10 (the cabinet stands in the middle, so each arm reaches its sub-task). Screening showed every other realistic edit left the pipeline >= 0.6; this one dropped it to 0.1.
rounds.why_missed: With the cabinet centred, the fixed assignment always gave each arm a reachable sub-task, and the object never lay in the drawer's path.
rounds.fix: Repairs (5 of 6, best 0.6; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): assign each sub-task to the arm nearer to it (possibly one arm for both); if the picking arm cannot reach the drawer, set the object down mid-table for the other arm; move the object itself out of the drawer's path before opening; fall back to the other arm when the nearer one cannot open the drawer, switching at the first table collision instead of re-grasping six times; the noise-robust stillness check from v8 again. Why unsolved: pulling at x = 0.24 the right arm's links strike the table after ~10 cm (2-4 kN) and the drawer springs back shut, while the left arm cannot reach the handle; this is the robot's reach and the simulator/planner behaviour at its edge, not something the pipeline can change.
rounds.general_rule: Assign each sub-task to the effector that can actually reach it (one effector may do several in sequence, or hand the object over through a free spot), treat the manipulated object itself as an obstacle to other sub-tasks, and switch effector or strategy at the first sign of a kinematic limit instead of retrying with the same one.

rounds.weakness: Same scene as unsolved v9 (cabinet 20 cm right), retried after backend v2 stopped the arm from grinding on the table. With the fixed rule 'drawer to the arm opposite the object', the far arm could not reach the handle; the near arm, gripping the bar at its centre far out to the side, pulled with a cramped wrist that sagged 6 cm into the table and slipped off the handle; a right-side object lay in the drawer's path; and a blocked retreat left the hand where going home swept the half-open drawer shut.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1/A10 (each arm can reach its sub-task). Screening showed this was the only realistic edit that still broke the round-3 pipeline; v9 had been abandoned at 0.6 because of the table-grinding backend bug.
rounds.why_missed: With the cabinet centred both arms reach the handle comfortably, so nearness and fixed roles were never questioned and the grip point on the handle bar never mattered.
rounds.fix: Four repairs on top of the v9 attempt (backend v2 throughout; v2d widened the force-limit release window for a hand pressed on the table to 0.4 s): sub-tasks go to the arm that reaches them, but for a handle far to one side the arm reaching across from the other side pulls (observed to track the pull cleanly where the near arm sags); the bar is gripped 6 cm from its centre towards the robot's centre line with a partly open, vertically closing grip; after a stall the pull continues in free-path slow steps; after letting go the hand lifts clear before backing off; the object is moved out of the drawer's path first if needed; and if the picking arm cannot reach the drawer it sets the object down mid-table for the other arm. Final: base 1.0, v1 0.9, v5 0.8, v6 0.9, v10 0.8.
rounds.general_rule: Choose the effector and the grip point for a forceful motion by how well the arm can carry it out there (a comfortable, uncramped configuration, observed from how it tracks), not by which effector is nearest or which grip point is nominal, and move clear of a just-released moving part before travelling so the travel cannot undo the work.

rounds.weakness: Every pick came straight down on the object and lifted straight up. A fixed shelf 1 cm above the tallest object made every top-down grasp unreachable (10/10).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A9/A5 at the pick (the space above the object is free). Objects on shelves and under counters are common.
rounds.why_missed: Nothing in the nominal scene is above the object.
rounds.fix: Repairs (2 of 6, best 0.0; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): detect an overhang above the object and pick from the side (fingers pointing away from the robot, opening sized to the object), draw the object out horizontally until clear, then lift; then pitch the approach 17-34 deg downward so the fingertips reach low objects while the wrist stays high and behind. Why unsolved: the free height under the shelf (11 cm) is about the height of the hand's wrist link, so approaches that reach the object put the wrist on the table (100-560 N, stopped by the force limit) or are unreachable, and 2-3 cm objects cannot be gripped from the side at all.
rounds.general_rule: Check the full hand envelope (wrist included, not just the fingers) against the free space around the target before choosing a grasp, and when no grasp fits, move the target first by non-prehensile means (drag it into the open) instead of forcing a grasp in place.

rounds.weakness: The pick assumed nothing rests on or leans against the object. With a light board lying on it, top-down grasps of the object were blocked and side grasps pushed the board and the cube; 7/10 failed.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A12/A5 at the pick (nothing rests on the object). Items covered by a lid, a sheet or another item are common, and screening showed it was the one remaining realistic edit that broke the round-4 pipeline (0.1).
rounds.why_missed: Nothing ever rested on the object in the nominal scene or in earlier variations.
rounds.fix: Repairs (5 of 6, best 0.5; marked unsolved, pipeline reverted): detect things resting on the object (bottom at its top, overlapping it) and take them off before the pick, set down >= 20 cm away; grip the lid from above only, first with the fingertips just above the object (too weak: it dragged the lid off sideways), then at the lid's mid-height with a slow straight lift; also clear anything left leaning against the object. A control without the lid scored 1.0. Why unsolved: the object is a 10 g cube; every slip of the lid or graze of a fingertip during removal makes the simulator fling it off the table (metres away), and the extra removal step pushes other seeds over the 120 s budget. Controls: the same cube and pose without the lid scored 1.0, and with the object at a realistic 200 g the frozen round-4 pipeline already scored 0.7 under the lid (it does not break). So v12's break, and its failure to recover, measured mostly the simulator's handling of a 10 g object under contact, not a robustness gap of the program.
rounds.general_rule: Before grasping, check what rests on or leans against the target and remove it with a firm grip and a straight, slow lift, then verify both that it is gone and that the target did not move, because a half-removed cover that slides off becomes an obstacle pressed against the target.

rejected.reason: invalid scene: seed 5: added object ground touches the robot at reset

rounds.weakness: The program measured both objects once at the start and grasped the second object several seconds later from that stale measurement. When the box was nudged 8 cm during the first grasp, the second grasp closed on empty air and the program gave up (0/10).
rounds.how_found: I questioned the assumption that objects stay where they were first measured until the arm reaches them. I suspected it because the second grasp starts about 4 s after the only measurement, and a real scene can be bumped in that time.
rounds.why_missed: In the base task nothing moves, so one measurement at t=0 is as good as a fresh one. Averaging eight detections made the stale estimate look precise, which hid that it could be out of date.
rounds.fix: Each object is now re-measured right before it is grasped, once two looks 0.3 s apart agree (it is at rest). After closing, the program checks that the fingers closed on something without being wedged open, and that the object rose with the lift; otherwise it retries with another grasp point. While recovering, the base task exposed two more fragile steps. (1) The scan pose is now computed from fresh measurements of both held objects instead of one open-loop placement. The free roll about the scan axis is chosen to keep the wrist near its start orientation, because the planner had reported success for a pose where the wrist folded into its own arm. (2) Every move is checked against the commanded pose.
rounds.general_rule: Act on a measurement taken right before the action, not one from the start: re-perceive an object when you are about to touch it, after it has come to rest, and afterwards confirm the action had its intended effect (object in hand, object lifted, arm actually at the commanded pose).

rounds.weakness: The box was always brought to one fixed meeting point in front of the robot, and the scanner was sent there without telling the planner about anything else on the table. A pole standing at that spot blocked half of the scans (5/10 failed).
rounds.how_found: I questioned the hard-coded meeting point: the program never looks at whether the space where the two hands meet is free. Real tables often have something standing in the middle.
rounds.why_missed: The base scene is empty above the table, so a constant meeting point always worked. I had copied the scripted expert's fixed target pose without asking where it came from.
rounds.fix: Candidate meeting points are now tested against the perceived obstacles, with the needed space sized from the measured box and scanner, and every move gives the obstacles to the planner. Moving the meeting point closer to the robot then folded the box arm's wrist into its own links while the planner still reported success. So the presentation now uses the box's free roll about its scan axis to keep the hand near its start orientation, checks that the arm arrived, and otherwise tries the next roll, then the next meeting point. The box's target orientation is defined by its scan-face direction, not by a fixed quaternion that the placement helper had never actually enforced.
rounds.general_rule: Never hard-code where an action happens: choose the spot from perceived free space sized from the measured objects, give the planner every obstacle, use any free degree of freedom of the goal (such as a roll that does not matter) to keep the arm in a natural posture, and confirm the arm actually arrived before continuing.

rounds.weakness: The arms were assigned from the scanner's side alone, and the box went to the other arm wherever it was. With both objects on the left (scanner near the middle, box far left), the right arm reached across the table for the box and failed (1/10).
rounds.how_found: I questioned the assumption that the two objects lie on opposite sides of the robot. Nothing in a real scene guarantees that, and the program never looks at where the second object is before committing an arm to it.
rounds.why_missed: The task's own randomisation always puts the objects on opposite sides, and the scripted expert decides from one object's side. I copied that rule without asking whether the layout could differ.
rounds.fix: Arms are now assigned jointly: for each of the two assignments, check that each object has a reachable grasp for its arm, and pick the feasible one with the least total sideways reach. Recovering also exposed two latent bugs in the scan loop. (1) Re-aiming searched only the four best-ranked rolls, so the chosen roll could drop out of the list and no correction happened. (2) Once corrections did happen, a tolerance tighter than the measurement noise triggered needless re-planned moves; one of them folded the wrist and knocked the scanner out of the hand. The final check now averages 20 detections and accepts within 1.2 cm (success allows 2.5 cm). Corrections are small straight-line moves instead of re-plans, and free meeting points away from the body are preferred over ones close to it.
rounds.general_rule: Decide which arm handles which object from where all objects actually are and whether each arm can reach its object, never from the position of one object alone.

rounds.weakness: After the first arm picked its object, it parked right above where the other arm had to reach. Each arm's planner knows nothing about the other arm, so with the box set down right in front of the scanner the second arm's wrist ran into the first arm's fingers (7/10 failed).
rounds.how_found: I questioned the assumption that the arm that has finished its pick never stands in the other arm's way. That holds only because the task normally puts the objects on opposite sides, and the planner models one arm at a time.
rounds.why_missed: The base layout keeps the two arms' workspaces apart, so a resting pose 'lifted above where I grasped' never got in the way of anything.
rounds.fix: After the first pick, the busy hand moves at least 25 cm (horizontally) away from the second object and up. If that move cannot be planned it tries alternatives: away from the object, back towards its own side, then straight up. The second arm's planner is given the object in the busy hand as an obstacle. Making the box an obstacle for the scanner grasp was tried and reverted: the inflated box blocked the scanner's only grasp approach.
rounds.general_rule: In two-arm work, treat the other arm and whatever it holds as an obstacle: before one arm works somewhere, move the other arm clear of that area, because each arm's planner does not know about the other.

rounds.weakness: With the box at the back edge of the arms' reach, four things went wrong. (1) The straight-line top-down approach could not be planned. (2) A lift that could not be planned was treated as a failed grasp, so the program opened the hand and dropped a box it was holding. (3) A side grasp's approach pushed the box off the table. (4) Carrying the box back and aiming the scanner from those far postures folded the wrists into the arm, which the planner does not model.
rounds.how_found: I questioned the assumption that every grasp, lift and carry is comfortably inside the arms' reach. A box put down at the back of the table is common, and the program had never been near the reach limit.
rounds.why_missed: All objects in the task start in a band near the robot, so no motion was ever close to the reach limit, and a planning failure had always meant 'blocked', never 'too far'.
rounds.fix: Six repairs: (1) alternative lifts that pull the object towards the body; (2) more grasp attempts; (3) when the straight approach cannot be planned, grasp 2 cm higher from a short approach; (4) that approach kept straight and verified (an unconstrained plan for a 1 cm move swung the whole arm into the robot's body); (5) returning to the start pose after a try that did not arrive (it helped here but made the close-together layout worse, 0.9 to 0.5); (6) dropping hand poses below table clearance. The best state reached v9 0.9 with another scene at 0.5, and the last 0.6. Unsolved; the pipeline was reverted to round 4.
rounds.general_rule: A motion that cannot be planned leaves the world unchanged: never undo progress (release a held object, abandon a grasp) because the planner said no; first try other motions that stay inside the reachable workspace, such as pulling the object towards the body.

rounds.weakness: When a tall object filled the whole usual meeting area, every spot on the short meeting list was blocked, and the program fell back to the default spot, which it knew to be blocked (0/10). Recovering also showed that grasps of objects a few cm from a tall obstacle are caught between two planner limits. With the obstacle in the planner's world, its coarse hand model refuses the straight approach; without it, the wrist really does hit the obstacle.
rounds.how_found: I questioned the assumption that some spot on the short list of meeting points is free, and that the default spot will do if none is.
rounds.why_missed: Round 2 replaced the fixed spot with a short list of alternatives and kept a fallback to the default. With one thin obstacle there was always a free entry, so the fallback was never exercised.
rounds.fix: Six repairs: (1) a grid of meeting points searched nearest-first, never falling back to a known-blocked spot (0.0 to 0.3); (2-3) giving a grasp and its lift only the obstacles near the object (0.3 to 0.6); (4) ranking height before depth for meeting points (0.8, but the close-together layout fell to 0.7); (5) always giving the planner what the other hand holds (all older scenes 0.8-1.0, v10 0.7); (6) a short-approach grasp fallback (v10 0.7, close-together layout 0.6). Unsolved; the pipeline was reverted to round 4.
rounds.general_rule: When the usual places are all blocked, search a wider space that is actually free (higher, further) instead of falling back to a default you already know is blocked; if nothing free is found, stop rather than act into a known collision.

rounds.weakness: The stack was always built at one hard-coded table spot. With a fixed box standing there, every attempt to put the base block down was refused by the planner ('no plan to pre-place') and the same spot was retried until the time budget ran out (10/10 seeds failed; RoboTwin's expert, which also uses a fixed spot, fails too). Repair exposed two more gaps: a spot that is merely clear is not enough, because the far arm could not reach across the body to spots 16 cm off-centre and spots behind the box made the forearm pass over it; and when the holding arm could not reach the target there was no fallback, so the block was dropped and a failed grasp by the far arm pushed another block off the table.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A1 (the build spot is empty). Clutter left exactly where the robot intends to work is the most common surprise on a real table, and the pipeline had no notion of choosing where to work.
rounds.why_missed: The task generator keeps that region free of objects, so the hard-coded spot always worked in the nominal scene and reachability by both arms was never in question.
rounds.fix: The build spot is now chosen at run time from a grid of table spots: at least 10 cm from the footprint of every perceived object that is not a task block, 12 cm from loose blocks, with a clear straight corridor from both arm bases, ranked by |x| (the far arm reaches across) and then by distance to the preferred spot. While holding the block the pipeline tries the ranked spots in order. If the holding arm reaches none of them, it sets the block down near the middle on its own side and the other arm takes the next try. A grasp the side arm cannot plan is retried with the other arm.
rounds.general_rule: Never hard-code where an object should go: choose the goal location at run time from perceived free space, require it to be reachable by every effector that must act there, keep ranked alternatives, and have a fallback (another effector or an intermediate set-down) when the current effector cannot reach.

rounds.weakness: The last block stood in a U of three light boxes with 1 cm gaps. The standard grasp picks one top-down wrist angle by preference, its open fingers would land on the boxes, and the planner refused every approach. The pipeline's only remedy for a blocked grasp was to move other task blocks, so it retried the same grasp until the 80 s budget ran out (0/10). Repair exposed two more gaps. With the finger line cleared, the planner's safety padding still refused to descend into the 1 cm gaps beside the fingers. And the extra clearing motions ran out the time budget, because the pipeline re-opened open grippers and re-homed arms that were already parked (1-2 s each).
rounds.how_found: Questioned A6'/A14 (only task objects can block a grasp, and some top-down grasp is always free). On a real table, clutter is often packed right against the object you want, and the pipeline had never looked at where its open fingers would go.
rounds.why_missed: The task generator keeps the blocks at least 10 cm apart with nothing else on the table, so the default grasp always had free space. The clearing code was written for the only blocking case that had occurred (another block).
rounds.fix: Before each grasp, the pipeline checks where the open fingers would land on both face-aligned finger axes, against every perceived object. It picks the axis with the fewest objects in the way and lifts those objects aside, using a manual top-down grasp tried at both wrist directions and setting them down on a free spot. Then it grasps along that axis, letting the final descent touch only neighbours that stand beside the fingers. Gripper and homing motions that would not change anything are skipped.
rounds.general_rule: Before grasping, check the space the open gripper will sweep against every perceived object (not just the ones the task names), choose the approach that needs the least clearing, move what is in the way, and accept contact only with neighbours that your own geometry check shows the fingers will clear.

rounds.weakness: The build spot was chosen once, at time 0, and reused on every try. A box that slid onto it 2 s later made every attempt to put the base block down fail ('no plan'), and the robot kept retrying the same stale spots until time ran out (s_break 0.3). Repair exposed three more costs. (1) The grasp fallback ladder tried the far arm, and an untilted top-down pose, even where neither can reach, and that burned the 80 s budget. (2) The planner's padded model of the hand refuses to come down within about 6-8 cm of a neighbour, so a contact allowance limited to 3 cm was useless. (3) Allowing contact on free-form or lifting paths let the arm swing through neighbours and fling 10 g blocks off the table.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A16 (the scene is static apart from the robot, so a location chosen at the start stays valid). In a shared workspace people put things down while the robot is working, and this pipeline computed its plan only once.
rounds.why_missed: Nothing moved in the earlier scenes, so computing the spot once at the start behaved exactly like recomputing it before each use.
rounds.fix: The build spot is now chosen right before every placement, from a fresh look. Before choosing, the pipeline waits (at most 3 s) until no perceived object moves more than 1 cm between looks 0.2 s apart. Verification is against the goal actually used. Also: the far arm is not tried for blocks beyond its reach; manual grasps try approaches tilted by 0.35 and 0.6 rad; descents among neighbours allow contact only on a short orientation-locked path; and lifts allow contact with neighbours only if a plain lift has no plan.
rounds.general_rule: Choose each goal location from a fresh observation taken immediately before acting on it, after waiting for the scene to stop moving, and never reuse a location chosen earlier in the episode.

rounds.weakness: The pipeline checked only the block it had just put down and never re-checked the stack. When the middle block was knocked off after passing its check, the pipeline stacked the top block onto the fallen block lying on the table and declared itself done (0/10). Repair exposed four more problems. (1) After a bump, a block could end up jammed against the hand, every plan from the current pose was refused, and the arm stayed stuck. (2) Without a precondition, most of the time budget went on putting a block onto a support that had just been knocked over; a first, naive precondition check made the two arms hand the block back and forth. (3) Checks with too few samples and a tolerance close to the noise level redid work that was already correct. (4) Every failed grasp variant paid for a lift and a fresh approach, although a refused plan had not moved the arm at all.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A17 (a block that passed its check stays put). In a real workspace a finished structure gets bumped by people, by the other arm, or by settling, and the pipeline checked each step once and then forgot it.
rounds.why_missed: In the earlier scenes nothing disturbed a finished step, so checking each step once looked sufficient. The cost of a disturbance only appeared when it hit between steps.
rounds.fix: The stack is now built in a closed loop. After every step the pipeline waits for the scene to settle and checks every relation of the goal from the bottom up, using 20-sample averages and tolerances inside the task's own. It sets aside anything resting on a misplaced block and redoes the lowest broken level. Before every placement it checks the target's precondition (the stack below is right); if that fails, it puts the held block down out of the way and returns to the loop. A jammed hand is freed by lifting straight up, with contact allowed only near the hand. After a refused plan the pipeline tries the next pose directly, without a lift and a fresh approach.
rounds.general_rule: Treat the goal as a set of relations to be re-verified as a whole after every action and before every action that depends on them, and repair the lowest broken relation first, instead of assuming that a step verified once stays done.

rounds.weakness: Every way the pipeline knew to free a block assumed it could reach the block from above: lift away whatever crowds it, then grasp top-down. With a fixed slab 1 cm above the block, the pipeline tried to lift the slab (it cannot move), then retried top-down grasps that the slab blocks, and ran out of time (0/10; RoboTwin's expert fails too). Repairs: (1) obstacles that do not rise when lifted are now remembered as immovable; (2) a non-prehensile push with the closed top-down hand did nothing, because a single long move_by was planned over the block rather than through it, and in short increments the palm (about 5 cm above the fingertips) hits the slab edge before the fingers reach the block; (3-4) dragging the block out with a horizontal side grasp works occasionally (best 0.2), but the hand must pass through the 6 cm gap between table and slab. Once the planner's padding is added, that gap is too small for most block orientations.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A21 (every block can be reached from above, or made reachable by lifting away what crowds it). Objects under shelves and in cubbies are common on real tables.
rounds.why_missed: Every earlier obstruction was beside the target and movable, so lifting it away was always enough. Nothing ever covered a target from above.
rounds.fix: Not recovered within the repair budget; the variation is marked unsolved and reverted, and the pipeline is back at its round-4 version. The remaining options (a horizontal or tilted hand in the 6 cm gap) all hit the same limit: the table is always in the planner's collision world with padding, so the pipeline cannot reach that pose reliably. Lessons kept for the harness: test whether an obstruction is movable before planning around moving it; a push needs short straight segments and a pusher whose whole body, not just its tip, clears the space the object leaves.
rounds.general_rule: Before planning to move an obstruction, test whether it can move at all, and before relying on a non-prehensile push or a side reach, check that the hand's full body (palm and wrist, not just the fingertips) fits through the space the object occupies, otherwise pick a different strategy early instead of spending the time budget on retries.

rounds.weakness: The table top was the only place the pipeline would work. Build and relay spots were always at table height, and every obstacle footprint was off-limits, even blocking the arms' corridors whatever the obstacle's height. With a broad, low, fixed tray filling the middle front of the table, no table spot was reachable by both arms and the relay band was covered. The base block could not be put down, failed placements opened the gripper and dropped blocks from height, and every seed ran out of time (0/10). RoboTwin's expert succeeds, because its fixed target happens to land on the tray top. Repair exposed a second limit: building on a raised surface uses up the arms' vertical reach. The top block of a stack on the 8 cm tray must be released around 1.0 m, at the edge of what a top-down hand can reach away from the body, so its placement often had no plan.
rounds.how_found: Questioned A22 (the table top is the only work surface). Real tables carry trays, boxes and books with flat tops, and people build on them all the time. The pipeline only ever looked for free *table*, so a flat obstacle counted purely as a loss of space.
rounds.why_missed: There was always free table near the middle, so a stable flat top never had to be considered, and stacks never got high enough to reach the arms' height limit.
rounds.fix: Candidate build spots now include the level tops of other objects: the top must be within about 11 deg of level and at least 9 cm wide, and the block centre must sit at least 3.5 cm inside its edges. The corridor check ignores objects lower than the work height (the arms reach over them). Placement allows contact only with the surface the block will rest on. On a raised surface the preferred spot moves towards the robot in proportion to the height, and high targets use a shorter pre-place approach. A block that cannot be placed is put back where it was picked up, instead of being dropped.
rounds.general_rule: Treat any stable, level, large-enough surface, not only the table, as a place to work or to hand objects over, but count its height against reach: the higher the work, the closer to the robot and the shorter the approach must be.

rounds.weakness: The program only ever approached the press point along a short straight corridor from the front (small yaw and pitch variants). With a movable box standing in front of the switch, every pre-press pose was in collision or unreachable, so it gave up after trying both arms (8 of 10 seeds). It never looked at what else stood between the hand and the target.
rounds.how_found: Listing assumptions, the straight free corridor in front of the press point (A4) was the one a real robot meets most often: objects are routinely left in front of switches and buttons. The planner already avoided known obstacles in transit, so I suspected the failure would come at the final approach, which has to come straight on.
rounds.why_missed: In every training scene the switch stood alone on the table, so approach failures came only from reach limits. I treated an unreachable approach as a reachability problem (try another arm or angle), not as a sign that the scene must be changed first.
rounds.fix: Before pressing, the program lists every detected object, other than the target, whose box overlaps the corridor in front of the press point. It grasps each one and sets it down to the side. If the grasp is impossible (on one switch model the object is only 1 cm from the switch, and wider than the gripper's opening), it sweeps the object sideways with the closed gripper pointing down. The sweep is lowered next to the object with contact allowed, tried with the hand both ways round about its pointing axis (one side of the wrist sticks out and collides), and counts even when the reach ends early, because the corridor is re-checked afterwards. Three repair iterations: 0.8 (grasp and set aside), 0.7 (sweep added, still refused near the switch), 1.0 (sweep start widened, contact allowed on the descent, both hand orientations).
rounds.general_rule: Before any contact motion, check the whole approach corridor for other objects and clear the movable ones first, grasping them or, when no grasp fits, pushing them aside along a path the arm can actually reach, and then re-check that the corridor is clear rather than assuming the clearing motion finished.

rounds.weakness: The program judged 'done' from one ambiguous signal: the rocker stopped turning between two small push stages. With a stiff rocker it stops turning for several other reasons: the fingertip slid off it, the arm was not pushing hard enough, the finger face was hitting the plate, or the planner refused the next stage. Each of these was read as 'at the stop'. Also, its small, position-controlled stages produced too little force, and its tilted pushes moved along the hand's axis and slid off.
rounds.how_found: The stop test (A5) rested on the mechanism being easy to move: a stall could only mean the end of travel. Real switches and buttons are often stiff, so I raised the joint's friction. Screening showed partial turns on 7 of 10 seeds. In-process traces of the fingertip depth, against the commanded depth and the true joint angle, then separated the failure modes.
rounds.why_missed: On the easy mechanism every stall happened at the true stop, so the single test was always right. I never asked what else a stall could mean, nor that a position-controlled arm applies force only through how far it is held back from its target.
rounds.fix: Five repair iterations. (1) A stall counts only if the fingertip is held back from its commanded depth: a fingertip that runs on freely has slipped off (0.4). (2) Push along the direction the mechanism gives way (horizontal), whatever the hand's tilt, and judge a stall only after this push has turned the rocker (0.6). (3) When held back without turning, command deeper targets: a larger position error pushes harder; the stop is accepted only when held back firmly (2.5 cm) (0.7). (4) Level approaches turned about the vertical come before tilted ones (a level finger face meets the rocker before the plate), and a stop is accepted only after a second, independent push from another approach finds no more travel (0.7, now out of time). (5) Cheaper presses (6 coarser stages, a shorter pre-press distance, likely approaches first) to fit the time budget (0.8; all scenes base 1.0 / v1 1.0 / v2 0.9).
rounds.general_rule: Never read 'it stopped moving' as 'it is done' from one push: tell apart the possible causes (end of travel, too little force, slipping off, being blocked elsewhere) by checking how far the tool was held back from its commanded target, push harder by commanding a deeper target when resistance is the cause, and confirm completion with a second, independent attempt that finds no further travel.

rounds.weakness: The program measured the target once, before moving the arm, and aimed every later push at that spot. When the switch slid 8 cm sideways while the arm was on its way, every push hit the empty air or the plate edge beside it (0 of 10).
rounds.how_found: A1 (the target stays where it was measured) was the remaining assumption with a direct line of code relying on it: the single detection at the start. Screening showed that sideways and backwards slides broke it (0.0 and 0.1), while reorienting or moving the switch before the start did not.
rounds.why_missed: In every earlier scene the target was fixed for the whole episode, and the only re-measurements were of the rocker angle, which was itself the progress signal. The target's position was never treated as something that can go stale.
rounds.fix: One repair. Before every press attempt the program locates the press point again. It takes two averaged looks 0.3 s apart and accepts the position only when they agree within 1.2 cm (the target is still). If the target moved since the last look, the next attempt aims at the new position and push direction. Scenes: base 1.0, v1 0.9, v2 0.9, v3 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Treat every target measurement as stale once the arm has moved: re-measure right before each contact attempt, accept the measurement only after two looks a moment apart agree (the target is still), and re-aim the attempt if it moved.

rounds.weakness: The corridor-clearing step trusted the grasp's success flag. On a 5 kg blocker the grasp closed (both fingers on the box), but the hand could not carry it, so place() failed. The step then reported 'not cleared' and returned without trying the sideways sweep that would have worked. Where the grasp did not close, the sweep ran and the press succeeded, but only after a slow failed carry attempt ate most of the budget.
rounds.how_found: The round-1 repair added a new assumption: whatever blocks the corridor can be moved by grasping or sweeping it. A heavy object in the way is common on a real bench, so I made v1's blocker 5 kg. An in-process trace with the box's true position showed the sweep does move it, while eval traces ended early with the box untouched after a 'successful' grasp.
rounds.why_missed: In round 1 every grasp that closed could also lift the object, so 'grasped' and 'movable' were the same thing, and the fallback chain was written to run only when the grasp itself failed.
rounds.fix: One repair. After grasping a blocker, lift it 3 cm and check that its detected height rose. If not, it is too heavy to carry: release, retreat, and sweep it instead. After every clearing attempt (carry or sweep, either side), re-check the corridor and continue with the next method until it is clear. Scenes: base 0.9, v1 1.0, v2 0.9, v3 1.0, v4 0.9.
rounds.general_rule: Do not take an action's success flag as its effect: after grasping something you intend to move, test that it actually moves with the hand before committing to the move, and when a method fails, fall through to the next method instead of ending the attempt.

rounds.weakness: The approach corridor was checked once, at the start. A box that slid into it 1.5 s later (after the check, before the first press) blocked every pre-press pose, and the program gave up after trying every approach with both arms (0 of 10).
rounds.how_found: The round-1 repair checks the corridor once; A9 (nothing enters the push path later) was still unattacked. Objects being put down in front of a target is common around people. Screening showed an arrival at 1.5 s broke it fully (0.0) and at 3 s nearly so (0.2), while an arrival during the press did not (0.9).
rounds.why_missed: After round 3 I re-measured the target before every attempt, but I still treated the rest of the scene as fixed once checked. The obstacles were measured once like the target used to be.
rounds.fix: One repair. Before every press attempt, check the corridor again and clear anything that has entered it (the same grasp / lift-test / sweep step as at the start), re-close the pressing hand if clearing used it, then re-locate the switch. Scenes: base 1.0, v1 1.0, v2 0.9, v3 1.0, v4 1.0, v5 1.0.
rounds.general_rule: Re-check the whole relevant scene, not only the target, right before each attempt: anything measured before the arm moved, obstacles included, may have changed.
